title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
I’m really excited about the new “ambient agent” concept. And at the same time — some companies have enjoyed similar work outputs for years. My experience and thoughts:
3 years ago, I released an email-to-ERP feature using the best tools available to us at the time. (OpenAI had just released ChatGPT.)
It was an automated email notification for our clients to send us missing shipment documentation. They just needed to reply to the email with an attachment, and then it’d get accepted by the system.
What these clients didn’t know was that, on the other end, our bot automatically uploaded these missing documents to the correct shipment — and from there, it kicked off an automated flow to process the document (generally OCR, because generally it was a PDF). This took < 5 minutes end-to-end.
In supply chain and logistics, “queue time” is a huge culprit of why orders or shipments get delayed. It’s the time when tasks sit in a queue, waiting for a 9-5 operator to do something as simple as upload the correct document to its corresponding shipment, which you need as an input for a broader goal like… clearing customs. So that your shipment then doesn’t miss its pre-booked trucking appointment to take it from port to warehouse. So that all of the following production- or sales-related dominoes can fall into place. Delays = lost money.
Here’s the thing, though, which gets me really excited about this new generation of ambient agents. I had a team of 4 engineers working on this for 4 months.
I’m now doing similar kinds of order processing work for CPG brands. It’s just me — a technical product manager and a Cursor IDE. (I taught myself to code many years ago, and never used it til now.) I learned all of those tough workflow lessons the first time, and now I can go even faster by sidestepping the pitfalls.
I’ve now shipped real solutions for real paying customers who, most importantly, cannot afford to pay 4 engineers + 1 pm for 4 months to get this done, the way that my former YCombinator unicorn employer could.
And that’s why I’m so bullish on this “ambient agent” concept… and especially as a startup company. In this case, the work was always possible, but just extremely expensive to do.

Thoughts on Agentic Orchestrations:
I think LangGraph is fundamentally better than any other agentic orchestration framework because of how useful just Graphs are.
Graphs are universal; every process executed by humans is graphical: iterative, cyclic, sequential—it's all a graph.
Pregel systems have been widely adopted and validated over the years. They show that almost no graphical system works better with a centralized state; you can always achieve the same result with shared, conversationally flowing state in graphs. LangGraph does something very similar with its shared state.
I experimented with AutoGen for a while, and it clearly lacked the kind of state management control you would need to build something useful.
I'm totally convinced that LangGraph is the correct way to think about your agentic system.
Draw it on paper first, then start coding—it works like a charm.

A breakthrough in AI agent testing: A novel framework for evaluating conversational agents. This open-source repo has everything you need!
Star this incredible project from Elad Levi & Ilan Kadar:
The framework is organized into these powerful components:
1. Policy Graph Builder - automatically maps your agent's rules
2. Scenario Generator - creates test cases from the policy graph
3. Database Generator - builds custom test environments
4. AI User Simulator - tests your agent like real users
5. LLM-based Critic - provides detailed performance analysis
It's fully compatible with LangGraph (@hwchase17), and they're working on integration with Crew AI and AutoGen!
They've already tested it with GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini, revealing fascinating insights about where these models excel and struggle.

I used to waste hours researching on the web for important information about any given company and its key decision-makers, nowadays I waste seconds...
My frustration led me to build an AI agent company researcher that crawls a company's website and searches the web, extracts key details, and generates a concise market research report—all automated and hands-free.
The main tech stack used to build this app are:
- @langchain's Langgraph and langsmith for building AI agentic workflows
- @firecrawl's new `/extract` endpoint for crawling and structured data extraction using natural language. Firecrawl also enables the agent to fetch more information about the company via web search.
Two of the key features of the app are:
- Ability for the agent to "fallback" to web search if it hasn't retrieved sufficient information from the url crawl extraction.
- Human review and editing of the style and format of the generated report by providing a prompt to AI for revision.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
⭐️Introducing the LangGraph Functional API
We spent a lot of time making LangGraph's state management (short/long term memory🧠, human in the loop🧑‍🤝‍🧑, time travel⏲️) production ready
You can now use these outside of the Graph syntax - with any framework (or none at all!)
With the release of the functional API, it is possible to get these features **without having to explicitly define a graph**
The functional API allows you to leverage LangGraph features using a more traditional programming paradigm, making it easier to build AI workflows that incorporate human-in-the-loop interactions, short-term and long-term memory, and streaming capabilities.
This API is complementary to the Graph API (StateGraph) and can be used in conjunction with it as both APIs use the same underlying runtime. This allows you to mix and match the two paradigms to create complex workflows that leverage the best of both worlds.

You can now use these outside of the Graph syntax - with any framework (or none at all!)

The functional API allows you to leverage LangGraph features using a more traditional programming paradigm, making it easier to build AI workflows that incorporate human-in-the-loop interactions, short-term and long-term memory, and streaming capabilities.
This API is complementary to the Graph API (StateGraph) and can be used in conjunction with it as both APIs use the same underlying runtime. This allows you to mix and match the two paradigms to create complex workflows that leverage the best of both worlds.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Retweet @rahulbhatia023
As AI technology evolves, base models will become commoditized, meaning they will be widely available, standardized, and undifferentiated. The real differentiator won’t be who has the best model, but who builds the strongest flywheel around it.
Here’s why:
- Open source providers and APIs make powerful models available to everyone.
- Cutting edge performance gains are becoming marginal, making differentiation harder.
- Cloud providers democratize compute power, reducing barriers to training or fine tuning models.
- Governments may create standardized safety and evaluation rules, making AI models more similar.
Winners will invest in FLYWHEELS. For AI companies, this means building moats around the model itself.
Think of base models as electricity: once commoditized, the value isn’t in generating power but in what you build with it. Similarly, AI’s future winners will be those who build the best 'applications + ecosystems' on top of commoditized models.
#AI #Innovation #FutureOfWork #LearnWithRB

How to build an open source deep research with @langchain Langgraph, @browserbase, @ExaAILabs, @firecrawl, and a carefully prompted @OpenAI o3-mini using structured output
how it works is probably close to:
user gives query
use o3-mini to assess query and identify any ambiguities
o3-mini creates initial plan ("ok I need to first look for this") which includes an initial query to make
Spin up multiple headless browsers in parallel with browserbase and search for articles using vanilla Google and Exa.
Crawl articles by either literally opening them in your headless browser, taking screenshots, and feeding them to o3-mini, or grabbing the text with firecrawl
Present the first results to o3-mini and prompt it to assess what info it now has, and what it now should look for,
repeat!

🤖Benchmarking Single Agent Performance
There's a lot of interest in multi-agent systems. To motivate the need for these, we put together some benchmarks for a **single agent**, trying to see at what point performance starts to degrade.
Learnings:
📉Both more context and more tools degrade agent performance
⛓️Agents that require longer trajectories degrade more quickly
🥇o1, o3-mini, and claude-3.5 sonnet are comparable and in a different league than gpt-4o and llama-3.3-70B
*⃣o3-mini performs as well as o1 and claude-3.5-sonnet with smaller context, but sees a steeper performance drop as context grows

I updated my AI hedge fund system diagram.
We now have 5 investor agents and 8 LLMs.
@langchain powers our agent graph.
Our AI agents:
1 • Ben Graham agent
2 • Bill Ackman agent
3 • Cathie Wood agent
4 • Charlie Munger agent
5 • Warren Buffett agent
You can mix + match these with any LLM.
Our LLM providers:
1 • Anthropic
2 • DeepSeek
3 • Meta
4 • OpenAI
5 • Google (coming soon)
6 • Mistral (coming soon)
No coding is required to run the system.
Everything is open source.
Here is how each investor agent works:
1 • Ben Graham: Uses classic principles like earnings stability, financial strength, and margin of safety with Graham Number calculations.
2 • Bill Ackman: Identifies durable competitive advantages, consistent cash flows, and strong financial discipline at a discount to intrinsic value.
3 • Cathie Wood: Identifies disruptive innovators, focusing on R&D intensity, expanding margins, and breakthrough technologies.
4 • Charlie Munger: Prioritizes business moats, management quality, and predictability while demanding a significant margin of safety.
5 • Warren Buffett: Focuses on owner earnings, consistent growth, and intrinsic value calculations with a long-term perspective on quality businesses.
Goal is to keep adding agents and LLMs.
Let me know what else to add.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Learn langgraph & langmem all in one course!
Quoting @AndrewYNg
New short course: Long-Term Agentic Memory with LangGraph. Learn to build an agent with long-term memory in this course developed in collaboration with @langchain taught by its Co-Founder and CEO, @hwchase17!
Personal assistance and productivity tasks have become important use cases for agents. An important feature of an AI assistant, such as a coding or calendar assistant, is its ability to keep improving over time from its experience. Agent memory is the key capability that enables this.
To add memory to an agent, you must first figure out what to store and what to retrieve when it is time to use the information. Additionally, you’ll have to decide when to update the stored information. For example, you might update in each iteration loop of the agent or perform updates in the background, with a helper agent.
In this course, you will learn a mental framework to build agents with long-term memory. You'll create a useful email assistant that can respond, ignore, and notify using writing, scheduling, and memory-management tools. You’ll develop your agent's memory by adding facts to its memory store, provide examples to learn the user's preferences, and optimize system prompts to evolve instructions based on previous responses.
In detail, you’ll:
- Learn how the three types of memory--semantic, episodic, and procedural–and the two update mechanisms–via hot path and in the background–apply to your agents.
- Build an email agent with writing, scheduling, and availability tools, along with a router that triages incoming email and handles it accordingly by ignoring, responding, or notifying the user.
- Add tools to your email agent that allow it to operate on semantic memory by learning facts about the user, storing them in a long-term memory store, and searching over them in future interactions.
- Incorporate episodic memory, in the form of few-shot examples, in the triage step of your agents to help them learn and update user preferences.
- Add procedural memory as system prompts, optimized with feedback to improve the instructions the agent follows.
Learn how to approach memory in agents, and start building agents with long-term memory with LangGraph!
Please sign up here:

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
I updated my AI hedge fund system diagram.
We now have 7 investor agents in our system.
@langchain glues everything together.
Our AI agents:
1 • Ben Graham agent
2 • Bill Ackman agent
3 • Cathie Wood agent
4 • Charlie Munger agent
5 • Phil Fisher agent
6 • Stan Druckenmiller agent
7 • Warren Buffett agent
No coding is required to run the hedge fund.
Everything is open source.
Here is how each investor agent works:
1 • Ben Graham: Uses classic principles like earnings stability, financial strength, and margin of safety with Graham Number calculations.
2 • Bill Ackman: Identifies durable competitive advantages, consistent cash flows, and strong financial discipline at a discount to intrinsic value.
3 • Cathie Wood: Identifies disruptive innovators, focusing on R&D intensity, expanding margins, and breakthrough technologies.
4 • Charlie Munger: Prioritizes business moats, management quality, and predictability while demanding a significant margin of safety.
5 • Phil Fisher: Prefers high-quality growth companies with excellent management, superior R&D capabilities, and consistent margins while performing thorough "scuttlebutt" research.
6 • Stan Druckenmiller: Seeks asymmetric risk-reward opportunities, emphasizing growth momentum and market sentiment.
7 • Warren Buffett: Focuses on owner earnings, consistent growth, and intrinsic value calculations with a long-term perspective on quality businesses.
I will keep adding new agents this week.

summary:
[1/3] Retweet @LangChain
Understanding multi-agent handoffs
Handoffs are a central concept in multi-agent systems.
LangGraph swarm is built on them.
But, they can be hard to understand.
Here, we break-down the swarm handoff mechanism.
📽️:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gnn3W93a4AA5xdH.jpg
────────
[2/3] Handoffs are a cool concept that enable "swarm" like architectures @RLanceMartin breaks them down in a simple way
────────
[3/3] Retweet @itamar_mar
Hot take on MCP🔥:
it isn't going to be the main protocol for agent-to-agent communication
MCP is basically a protocol that is designed to standardize how agents communicate with tools that are commonly used to fetch relevant/critical context needed for the agent to provide accurate answers
And that’s exactly my point:
MCP was built to help agents fetch context.
Not necessarily to support agent-to-agent communication
2 use cases where MCP doesn't handle well:
1> Agent 1 asks Agent 2 for help,
and Agent 2 needs to take over the user interaction to complete the task.
MCP doesn’t support such a handshake/handoff
2> Agent 1 and Agent 2 need to work on shared memory.
While MCP enables you to hack that,
we need a standard way to do that.
Where different developers building different agents can share memory without humans stepping in.
This kind of workaround shows us that MCP probably won’t be the protocol that defines this space
I think of MCP-1 a bit like USB-1.
And, the jump from USB-1 to USB-2 was not a game-changer.
So, while we are expecting the "MCP/USB-2" of agent protocols,
I believe a new, better and different protocol will emerge to really solve for the agent-to-agent communication

📢 New @auth0 product: Auth for GenAI 🤖 our new product for devs building apps with GenAI
It helps devs secure their GenAI apps, with the dev experience @auth0 is known for
You can start using Auth for GenAI today: auth0 dot ai
What's in the box?
This developer preview supports 4 use cases:
1️⃣ User Authentication
2️⃣ Calling APIs on the users' behalf
3️⃣ Async User Confirmation
4️⃣ Authorization for RAG
1️⃣ User Authentication
GenAI agents or apps still need to know who the user is. e.g. a chatbot might need to display chat history, or know the user age/country to customize replies This requires authentication, and Auth for GenAI makes it easy to implement in GenAI apps
2️⃣ Calling APIs on the users' behalf
GenAI apps interact with other apps, e.g. to read emails or send a pull-request And they don't need a UI Agents need to call APIs with credentials that are for a single user, with narrow permissions
3️⃣ Async User Confirmation
Many GenAI workflows are async, take "longer" to reply @OpenAI's o family of models is a good example of it. Users won't wait in front of a chat window. GenAI agents need to support async confirmation securely
4️⃣ Authorization for RAG
GenAI apps use RAG to make relevant data available to LLMs for replies To avoid disclosing sensitive information, it is paramount to ensure that the content used to generate answers is content each user can access
How do we make all of this easy?
We have SDKs, docs and sample apps for many of the popular GenAI app frameworks: @aisdk @langchain @llama_index @Firebase Genkit and others like @CloudflareDev AI and @crewAIInc are coming soon
And we really want your feedback (my DMs are open, we have a Discord community). If you have issues, want other features, frameworks, or want to collaborate on making Auth for GenAI easy to integrate into your platform, I'd love to chat
I am very excited about how this product will enable all of us devs to make prod ready AI apps a reality. Looking forward to learning how you are using it!

I'm a huge fan of OpenAI, but this is bad.
Evals that lock you into a single LLM provider defeat the entire purpose of an evaluation platform. In a world where LLM benchmarks and leaderboards are being gamed and increasingly meaningless, running your own evals (across models) on the tasks you care about matters more than ever.
So while I commend OpenAI for making LLMops potentially more convenient, I don't recommend locking yourself into this platform.
Quoting @OpenAIDevs
Introducing the Evals API.
You can now programmatically define tests, automate evaluation runs, and quickly iterate on prompts.
Evals are still available in the dashboard—and now through the API, so you can integrate them anywhere in your workflow.

I've recently open sourced a personal project that explores how AI can be applied to trading decisions.
BiBot-AI is a trading bot for @binance Futures that demonstrates the potential of AI agents in financial applications.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Great example of generate -> validate loop + error analysis
> "the most effective route to improve outcomes was brute force: retry steps until they passed or reached a limit. We give the validation errors ... to the LLM and built a loop runner"
> "1. Run failing files to find common issues.
2. Select a sample of files with a common issue.
3. Update prompts and scripts to address that issue.
4. Re-run against the sample of files to validate fix.
5. Repeat by running against remaining files.
After running this “sample, tune, sweep” loop for 4 days ... completed files from 75% to 97% of the total files, and had just under 100 files remaining"
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GodPg7aWYAAR4SF.jpg

OK, the AI Agent architecture is largely settled, with well-defined elements like one or more Language Models acting as the backbone, a model that facilitates reasoning and acting.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Love Charles' framing of 💤 sleep-time compute! It captures a similar idea to something LangMem labels as "subconcious" or "background" memory processing [1], where you schedule reflective work to be done, potentially after an agent or thread "goes to sleep".
Quoting @charlespacker
💤 sleep-time compute: make your machines think while they sleep ->
over the past several months we (at @Letta_AI) have been exploring how effectively utilize "sleep time" to scale compute.
the concept of "sleep-time compute" is deeply tied to memory - applying compute at sleep-time is only possible if your agent has persistent state which can continuously re-written with additional compute cycles.
in fact, the concept of "heartbeats" in MemGPT was actually inspired by the idea of an AI receiving heartbeats to "awake" it during sleep.
prior to MemGPT's release, I actually spent many weeks trying to perfect heartbeats to try and get the agent to learn something useful during its downtime - but never quite got it to work quite right 😅
our new sleep-time agent design in @Letta_AI takes the heartbeats idea to next level and allows you to arbitrarily scale the amount of compute you want to apply at sleep-time with multiple agents with memory wired together.
while one agent sleeps, a fleet of agents can work to re-assemble its memory asynchronously in the background

summary: 🔥hot take im workshoping, would love feedback when thinking about multi agent architectures it's useful to think about two different types of agents: - chat agents: messages in, messages out - task agents: structured output in, structured output out what is different? - task agents can be called as tools while chat agents need a more handoff mechanism - task agents likely will be longer running than chat agents - task agents are more likely to not need followups (call it once, get back a result, don't care about calling that thread again), chat agents obviously need followups - for task agents, if it returns a response that means it done, for chat agents if it returns a response that could be the final answer OR it could be asking the user a follow up question - task agents can still get human input through something like `interrupt` in LangGraph, and its very clear that is human input. chat agents likely will use a message response to get that input, unclear what that is (clarifying question or final answer) why does this matter? - should an agent protocol try to cover both types of agents or just one? - is MCP suitable for task agents?

🚀 Happy to introduce Daily Vibe Casting: a daily AI-generated podcast covering the most viral 𝕏 posts from the previous 24 hours
Drops daily on @vibecastingapp

Would love feedback, podcast link in comments
Why I built this? 👇
So I thought, what if I could turn 𝕏’s daily chaos into a podcast? I describe vibe casting (like vibe coding) as generating AI podcasts by throwing context into AI tools and producing audio from it
I’ve been iterating with the AI podcast generation for nearly a month, monitoring 𝕏 to find the most viral posts and feeding them into @NotebookLM to generate the podcast. I’m also using @langchain to automate the workflow and the whole process is now 99% automated
I recognise its current state could be a bit cringe at times but I'm sure it will get better over time
I spend a lot of time doomscrolling on 𝕏 and wanted something that could quickly catch me up on anything I might have missed. Like a highlight reel but in audio
I've always been a fan of radio and podcasts, especially fast-paced news radio shows like bloomberg or similar. It just made sense to have something with that same pace for 𝕏, the kind of thing that keeps us glued to the platform. - @btaylor on becoming Facebook CTO at age 29, pricing/packaging agents, and advice for application layer founders
- @DrJimFan of NVIDIA on why simulation is the key to robots passing the physical Turing test
- @ChaseLochmiller of Crusoe on the moving industrial bottlenecks to scaling AI: power, steel, real estate
- @mikeyk of Anthropic on MCP, Claude Code, and on his framework for product-building when the models themselves are changing so quickly

- @danintheory of OpenAI on how RL is going from the "cherry on top" of the pre-training cake to the main course, and what questions einstein-v1907-super-high might be able to answer by scaling reasoning compute
- @gradypb on the new physics of distribution, the Leone merchandising cycle applied to AI foundation models vs application startups, and his advice to startups to "run like heck"
- @Konstantine on the agent economy and stochastic mindset

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
The first real blueprint for AI that works in the background and just gets stuff done. Ambient agents scale because they’re event-triggered, not chat-bound. Langgraph orchestrates, Langsmith debugs. Do yourself a favor.
@hwchase17 @langchain
Quoting @sonyatweetybird
@hwchase17 of @langchain:
* Ambient agents are agents that listen to an event stream and act on it
* Ambient agents are event-triggered and concurrent.
Unlike chat agents, they act in response to background events and can run thousands of concurrent instances. They handle complex, multi-step tasks with human oversight.
* LangGraph and LangSmith are being built to support ambient agent infrastructure. LangGraph focuses on event-driven, bursty agent workflows; LangSmith adds observability and debugging for long-running agents.
* Human-in-the-loop design improves results, trust, and learning. Interaction patterns (approvals, edits, answering questions, time travel debugging) make ambient agents more reliable and adaptable. At LangChain we built this concept of an AgentInbox, where an agent can send things to the human for review

The Future of AI: Insights from Experts and Innovators
📢 Most Important Point:
AI is evolving beyond traditional paradigms, with a focus on system prompt learning, agentic architectures, and visual generative interfaces. These advancements are reshaping how we interact with technology and solve complex problems.
🚀 Technical Highlights:
- System Prompt Learning: A new paradigm where LLMs learn explicit problem-solving strategies through system prompts, enhancing data efficiency and adaptability.
- Agentic Architectures: Frameworks like LangGraph and Open Agent Platform are enabling reliable task delegation and multi-agent workflows.
- Visual Generative Interfaces: Future AI interactions will likely move from text-based terminals to dynamic, interactive 2D canvases tailored to user prompts.
💡 Insightful Perspective:
AI development is shifting from knowledge acquisition to habitual behavior and problem-solving strategies. This mirrors human learning, where notes and explicit strategies guide future actions.
⚡ Industry Impact:
These innovations are transforming industries by enabling faster prototyping, more reliable automation, and personalized user experiences. The rise of agentic systems is particularly impactful in fields like document processing, campaign creation, and research.
🎙️ Expert Opinions:
- @karpathy: “System prompt learning could be a new, powerful paradigm for LLMs, resembling RL but with explicit knowledge editing.”
- @hwchase17: “Agent observability and structured workflows are key to building reliable and scalable AI systems.”
- @AndrewYNg: “Avoiding coding is the worst career advice ever; technical skills remain crucial in the AI era.”
🧠 One-Line Takeaway:
The future of AI lies in adaptive learning, agentic systems, and visual interfaces, marking a shift from static models to dynamic, problem-solving collaborators.

We just wrapped up @langchain Interrupt, and here are my 10 key takeaways!
1️⃣ Agents are Here - I'm definitely riding a post-conference high. The energy was electric, and everyone was deeply engaged. The conference showcased real-world agent implementations happening now, such as AI SDRs, AI code writers, research agents, legal assistants, sales support, and more. These are agents in production at startups and enterprises, and not just digital natives.
2️⃣ Evals are Critical - Evals is the process of using fixture data to test an agent's performance with specific prompts. Every demo and discussion emphasized starting with Evals. This is a place where traditional design will truly shine. Designers are experts at capturing the human processes through journey mapping. This will be foundational to every agent. Evals are also a natural transition from TDD to a new process, Eval Driven Development (EDD). By embedding evals into the SDLC, running them at every commit, PR, and CI, developers gain the freedom to iterate confidently on code, agents, and prompts.
3️⃣ Architectures are Critical - Unlike traditional software, agent architectures cannot evolve haphazardly; they must be intentional from day one. Understanding how decisions, tool calls, and state are managed is essential. Migration between architectures is challenging, so starting with intentional, eval-backed designs is crucial.
Particularly popular architectures are supervisor and swarm multi-agent setups, and sub-agent graphs. Supervisor architectures oversee multiple sub-agents, ensuring cohesive task execution and error management. Swarm architectures utilize many agents working in parallel, leveraging distributed intelligence to complete complex tasks efficiently. Sub-agent graphs define clear interactions and responsibilities among agents, essential for larger, interconnected tasks.
Agents generally fall into two categories: Active Agents (like ChatGPT), requiring rapid, responsive interactions, and Ambient Agents, performing complex tasks in the background with a focus on accuracy and completeness.
4️⃣ Human-in-the-loop is essential - Thoughtfully integrating humans is more than oversight; it involves using human interactions to continuously improve agents through added memory and feedback loops. This transforms human roles from task execution to task management, elevating both human and agent effectiveness.
5️⃣ Think of agents as people, not systems - Companies using Ambient Agents often personalize them, assigning human-like roles and RBAC permissions instead of typical service-level integrations.
6️⃣ AI Driven Development is here to stay - AIDD is Revolutionizing and accelerating development processes.
7️⃣ Software surrounding agents is complex yet essential - The agent graph forms the application's core intelligence, but the real complexity lies in custom tool-building and integrations. These integrations, be it through MCP, model binding, or dedicated services, demand thoughtful decision-making regarding technology choices, deployment methods, and SDK or service approaches. These tools must be robust, observable, and thoroughly tested just like any traditional software.
8️⃣ Observability from day one is non-negotiable - LangSmith offers foundational visibility into agent workflows, critical given agents' probabilistic behaviors. Traditional debugging methods like print statements fall short; spans, traces, and comprehensive monitoring are essential. As observability evolves, LLMs will increasingly assist in alerting developers and operations to anomalies. Enhanced observability directly fuels more accurate evals and refined prompts.
9️⃣ Clear metrics are vital - Defining success and acceptable accuracy thresholds helps refine agents and demonstrates value. Unlike traditional software, an agent’s success is measured directly against human performance.
🔟 Agent Engineer/Designer the new job title - This emerging role merges prompting, product management, machine learning, software development, and UX journey mapping. Agent development requires great software. Effective prompting relies on understanding LLM reasoning, while practical ML skills enable fine-tuning and embedding models effectively. A product expertise ensures alignment with workflows and KPIs.
We're more ready than ever to stay focused on agentic AI. You'll find us building smart, intentional agents that integrate seamlessly into our customers' systems and drive real results. The work starts now!
Thanks @hwchase17 and team for a great conference!

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Memory is not the ultimate AI model lock in mechanism. A friend and I spoke about this at length last night. I initially thought it was but after discussing with this person for a bit about both of our personal experiences, we concluded that it's just not (yet), despite that being the currently prevailing belief.
Today, the thing that matters most about the model is that it gives you the right answer, full stop. Memory and additional context can help with that, but it certainly doesn't guarantee it.
Personal example: I was using one of the major model providers to help me understand a recent medical test. This model had all my previous tests, blood work, history, etc, but it completely misread the image. Just flat out misinterpreted it on multiple tries. It was like it was trying to tell me that the sky was not blue.
So what did I do? I just went over to their competitor and it nailed the result instantly. I ported all my results and history over in 2 minutes and have being using that model ever since.
Today, the model's number one job is accuracy and securing your trust, not personalization.

💹 Track costs across multi-modal inputs and token-caching
Cost tracking is essential for agentic applications because resource usage is determined dynamically by the agent itself. This is becoming trickier now that model providers charge different per-token prices by token modality, cache type, reasoning, etc.
LangSmith can now track costs for arbitrary token types so that you know exactly how much you're spending, no matter which models and which features you're using.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
These guys are building @langchain LangGraph Dynamic Graphs and caching to choose between 1000+ available MCP Servers as tools.
🔥
Quoting @sgviera
While exploring the new MCP-as-apps paradigm, my team and I hit a key challenge: with thousands of tools available, how does an agent reliably pick the right one for the task?
To tackle this, we built dynamic graphs using LangGraph (@langchain ), powered by a retrieval system that semantically matches user requests to tool definitions.
Once we select the tools, we check if there’s already a LangGraph graph with that combination cached — if so, we reuse it. If not, we create a new one. This caching mechanism lets us save significant resources while keeping performance high.
The result: better tool selection, fewer hallucinations, and way more efficient agents.
We’re all in on the MCP-native apps vision — and we’re building to make it truly scalable.

Traversal is tackling one of tech’s most stubborn problems: when production software systems go down, why is it still so hard—even with all our dashboards and data—to find the root cause, fast?
For my co-founders Raj Agrawal, Raaz Dwivedi, Ahmed Lone, and me, this is a deeply personal problem: we've seen how hard this problem is to solve, but also why it’s the perfect problem for us to solve together.
Traversal is building the AI Site Reliability Engineer (SRE) for the enterprise: the only AI agent that can autonomously troubleshoot, remediate, and even prevent complex production incidents. Our architecture pushes the frontier of AI agents and combines it with our research in causal machine learning to pinpoint the true root cause—not just symptoms—in real-time.
At 99.9% uptime, you get less than 44 minutes of downtime per month. Our agent is engineered to operate within that margin—scaling with your infrastructure to keep you well below the line, learning from your systems, telemetry, and incidents to improve continuously.
And it’s already working: @digitalocean, @eventbrite, @Cloudways, and more in the Fortune 100 trust Traversal as their first line of defense, with >90% accuracy on hundreds of high-impact incidents—freeing engineers from endless “dashboard dumpster diving.”

I have a ton of prompting/agent building tips to share based on my learnings from the agent I'm building now.

[2/2] Retweet @BraceSproul
Including few-shot examples in your prompt can help a ton, if done right. But if done incorrectly, it can cause the LLM to generate the exact opposite of what you want.
For example, I'm building a planning agent, and decided to add some *negative* few-shot examples (e.g. `Avoid generate plans like this: "..."`), and after wresting with the prompt for way too long, I realized the problem wasn't in my examples themselves. It was that I was giving it *negative* examples.
When I switched from *negative* few-shots to *positive* few-shots (e.g. `Your tasks should be formatted in this way: "..."`) it started following my instructions to a T, and planning in the way I want.
What did I learn from this?
*Negative* few-shots will hurt your prompt more than they'll help. You should avoid telling the model what *not to do*, and instead just tell it *what to do*. (OpenAI & Anthropic have both released prompting guides which back this claim up too)

title: @hwchase17
summary: 📃The rise of context engineering "Context engineering" has been an increasingly popular term used to describe a lot of the system building that AI engineers do But what is it exactly? The definition I like: "Context engineering is building dynamic systems to provide the right information and tools in the right format such that the LLM can plausibly accomplish the task." Builds upon takes from @tobi @dexhorthy @walden_yan @ankrgyl Not a new concept - agent builders have been doing it for the past year or two, and a lot of the tools we've build (LangGraph, LangSmith) have been built to assist with it. But it's a new term which will hopefully draw new attention to the skills and tools needed to do this properly.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Today I'm going to talk about conversation history management and summarization. The example below comes from the same `planner` sub-agent discussed yesterday. This is one of the many sub-agents which make up a coding agent we'll be open sourcing soon!
The `planner` agent is tasked with taking "read only" actions to gather context. These runs can get very long (sometimes the planner calls more tools than the programmer!), and we don't want to persist the entire planning conversation history when I hand it off to the programmer.
At first, I had it "summarize" the conversation history. This worked reasonably well, but the summaries weren't very high quality, and often only included surface level details. I struggled to get it to be general, while still including technical details without very strict prompting (which had other downsides).
Once I updated the LLM call which generates the summaries to instead instruct it to take "technical notes" and renamed the tool it was supposed to call to `write_technical_notes`, the quality of these summaries increased very obviously. I suspect this is due to two things:
1. I don't actually want the agent to summarize the entire conversation history. What I really want is for it to extract useful context from the conversation history, while ignoring simple/low priority context. When I prompt it to summarize, it tries to condense the entire conversation history, giving the same weight to both unimportant/irrelevant context, as it does to high quality and important context. Once I dropped all mentions of "summary" it stopped trying to condense all of the history, and instead focused on the technical details of which it would find most useful when actually executing the plan.
2. I believe the inclusion of "notes" helped with the quality of its output too. This is similar to the above, where I don't want it to summarize everything, but instead extract the highest quality context. In calling it a "note taking" task, it caused the LLM to act as a human note taker would, which meant it only writes down enough context to jog its memory later on, which is the most important context and omitting any intermediate and not necessarily highly relevant information.
These two findings reinforce the theory that naming your prompts/tools matters a lot. Even though most of the prompt for the note taker remains the same, the updates changing "summary" -> "note taker" was enough to change the structure of the output, along with what context from the conversation history it decided to include.
If you found this interesting, stick around for tomorrow's post where I'll discuss how I format conversation history in these summarization prompts (and others), along with other weird differences in the generations depending on how the conversation history was formatted in the prompt!

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
In today’s edition of Agent Activities, we’ll continue with the theme of context/conversation history management and discuss the pros and cons of different formatting techniques.
One of the sub-agents in the coding agent I’m building is the ‘programmer’. This is the main executor in the coding agent’s flow and is responsible for executing each of the tasks the planner generated. Because of this, it has a fairly complex flow with many unique LLM calls, tools, and prompts. Very quickly, I discovered I couldn’t just pass the full message history to the LLM for each of these steps, even if it fit within the context window. This is due to two main reasons:
Problem 1: The programmer has many individual steps, each with different tools. For the main action execution node, we always pass it the full conversation history via unmodified messages and a handful of tools. After calling and executing a tool (taking an action), we route to a simple LLM call with a single tool available to determine whether this last action successfully completed the current task. Even though the model was only provided one tool and “forced” (using the API to force tool use), it would still frequently hallucinate tools it didn’t have access to but that appeared in the message history. This led to obvious problems.
To combat this, I started stringifying all of the messages in the conversation history (wrapping the role, content, and tool calls in XML tags) and providing the entire history as a string via a single user message containing a prefix along the lines of: “Here is the full conversation history… {history}”. Stringifying the message history fixed the hallucinating problem altogether, and from then on, the LLM was always able to call the proper tool provided to it without hallucinating tools that appeared in the conversation history.
Problem 2: Similarly, I have some steps throughout the sub-agents that are used for summarization/note-taking/context extraction. When providing these LLM calls with the full conversation history as unmodified messages, they would constantly hallucinate outputs, tool calls, or outright ignore the system prompt. No matter how much prompt engineering I did in the system prompt, there would always be a case where I would, for example, ask it to take notes on some messages. Instead of taking notes, it would see that recent messages were writing files and would generate a response to that conversation history instead of listening to my system prompt and only taking notes on the provided message history. Just like I outlined above, when I switched to passing a stringified version of the message history via a user message, these issues were resolved.
I suspect these problems are caused by internal formatting of conversation history and/or tool calls + results that OpenAI/Anthropic do for us when we provide message histories, which cause the LLM to believe it still had access to said tools or weigh the conversation history higher than the system prompt.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
About three months ago we launched DGi ( a data agentic system. IT SUCKED, like all agentic systems do right now when it comes to data analytics.
Just a few weeks ago, I used one of the big AI players to vibe code a data dashboard. A few days later, I realized it was completely wrong. That’s the hard part about AI, we’re starting to rely on it so much that we end up living inside its hallucinations.
What we need are systems we can trust. That’s the real challenge.
Customers loved the idea behind DGi, but they told us it was unusable: too slow, inaccurate, and hard to rely on. The concept was right, but the execution wasn’t there yet.
We went back to the drawing board and decided that to make something people actually use, we had to:
Make it fast.
Make it secure.
Make it accurate, and give ourselves a way to measure that.
Specialize it with the right tools for real data analysis.
Today we’re announcing DGi v2, along with a performance evaluation comparing DGi to four other companies on real data analytics tasks (Replit, v0, Claude and OpenAI). You can see the summary of the results in the comments and in the image attached the overall benchmark.
DGi v2 now includes double envelope encryption, encryption on top of encryption. When you connect your database, your credentials go through two layers of protection.
We also trained DGi using gold-standard data science practices so it can better handle edge cases, large datasets, and more.
And we’re adding features like scheduling (coming next week), code editing, and a metadata store (credential storage), so AI can help, but you can step in and take control when needed.
We’re still far from where we want to be. Next up: dashboard creation and deployment. But this version is a solid foundation to start exploring and analyzing your data with a high level of accuracy and reliabillity.
Right now, DGi is somewhere between ChatGPT, Airflow, and Replit, but with deep data specialization. Our models are trained with data analysis best practices and include data reviews on final responses.
We hope you’ll keep supporting us on this journey. We imagine a future without Excel files, Power BI, or Tableau dashboards.
That future isn’t easy to build. Reliable and accurate agentic systems are complex to build. But we’re leading the way.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Building Async ("Ambient") Agents
Happy to share new, free course on building "ambient" agents! This is one of the most interesting agent UX patterns (e.g., Devin, Codex), allowing the agent to do work "in the background" and interact with the user via human-in-the-loop for select actions / approvals.
Course builds towards a concrete application -- an assistant that can autonomously run your gmail -- in a few steps, but the principles can be applied to other types of "ambient" agents beyond email.
Course starts with basics of building agents, setting up a simple router + email response agent -
Then moves to fundamentals of agent evaluation, using llm-as-judge as well as heuristic evals -
Then it adds human in the loop for approval of specific tool calls (e.g., actually sending the email) -
Finally, it adds simple memory to remember the human-in-the-loop feedback -
At the end, it show how to deploy the agent and connects to actual gmail tools. I've been using this to run my email for a few months.
You can find course link w/ all videos here. Many thanks to @labdmitriy to helpful feedback + review!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GuYkHS1aEAACvzn.jpg

5. Based on the MVP & eval results, build it out to be much more involved to improve results (will become expensive on a per run basis, but this will be improved on in the next step)
6. After building out a more complex and better preforming agent, see where you can simplify while still maintaining performance
7. More evals based on this simplified version
8. Production
High level:
Idea -> inspiration -> MVP agent -> evals -> complex agent -> simplified agent -> evals -> production

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
When I’m not shitposting, I actually spend a lot of time building AI products.
I haven’t shared much recently because a lot of my projects are behind tight NDA.
But I want to share my framework for building AI agents/software.
1/ Be experiment driven
AI development is incredibly experiment driven. When I approach a new problem, I generally don’t know how I’m going to solve it, I only have an intuition of reasonable approaches and experiments to run. This is notably different from traditional software development.
It is important to set up a set of evaluation or test cases you can use to align with stakeholders and/or develop against.
Determine the variables you need to test. For a more creative task, this may be the model I’m using. For a retrieval task, this could be testing agentic search vs traditional RAG, or the embedding model I use. For agents, this may be architectural decisions and level of flexibility vs determinism your task allows.
Most importantly, be ok not knowing what the destination looks like. Be good at designing the journey.
2/ Evals suck
I know evals suck. It’s annoying. I don’t really like doing it. It sometimes feels like pulling teeth trying to align with non technical stakeholders. HOWEVER, it’s really important for progress. Don’t over think evals. Just set up a simple and reliable process you can use to evaluate and compare the results of your experiments. You don’t need fancy tools, you only really need google sheets.
3/ Use open source resources
There are a ton of really great open source resources you can use to get started. I enjoy a lot of @BraceSproul’s content. For examples I am using his open deep research repo right now for an adjacent, but different use case.
4/ Prompting goes a long way
Most AI products are simply a combination of context management and prompt engineering. Good prompting goes a really long way. Think deeply about the prompt your LLM will see and the task you want it to complete. Does it make sense? It is clear? Would a human even understand? This goes a lot further than thinking through complex multi agent hierarchical systems (lol). Nail your prompt.
5/ The hardest part ..
The hardest part, and temptation, is to go to a person and say “what do you do”, and the try to automate that exact same process with AI. This is so hard and absolutely suboptimal. I have moved away from this approach, and started considering how to achieve the same outcome but with a different, AI first, process with human in the loop thoughtfully built in. Working with people who aren’t in AI, to build AI products, is really really fucking hard. Change management is hard too. Be wary.
6/ Build for the future
This is a personal preference of mine and could be wrong, but, build for the future.
Every AI product is a balance between determinism and flexibility. A linear workflow is deterministic. A tool calling agent is flexible. The tool calling agent may underperform now, but will improve as models improve and eventually significantly outperform linear workflows. I prefer to build for the latter, to ensure my products are future safe, and grow with the current state of progress and investment.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Context Engineering
@dbreunig and I did a meetup on context engineering last night. Wanted to share slides (below) + a recap of some themes / discussion points.
1/ Context grows w/ agents. @manusai mentions typical task requires ~50 tool calls.
2/ Performance drops as context grows. @kellyhongsn + @trychroma showed this very nicely.
3/ @dbreunig highlights that new buzzwords ("context eng") identify common experiences. Many of us built agents this year and had challenges wrt managing context. @karpathy distilled this well back in May.
4/ Many are sharing their experiences in blogs, etc but no common philosophy yet. "Pre-HTML era". Still, some common themes are emerging.
6/ Offload context. Use file system to offload context. @manusai writes at the start of a task and re-writes it during the task. They found that recitation of agent objective is helpful. Anthropic multi-agent writes research plan to file so it can be retrieved as needed and preserved. Manus offloads tok heavy tool observations.
7/ Reduce context. Summarize / prune messages / tool observations. Seen across many examples. Anthropic multi-agent summarizes the work of each sub agent. We use it w/ open deep research to prune tool feedback.
8/ Retrieve context. RAG has been a major theme w/ LLM apps for several years. @_mohansolo (Windsurf) and Cursor team have shared interesting insights on what it takes to perform RAG w/ prod code agents. On Lex pod, @mntruell (Cursor) + team talk about Preempt to assemble retrievals into prompts. Clearly have been doing "context eng" since well before the term.
9/ Isolate context. A lot of interest in using multi-agent systems to isolate context. @barry_zyj + co (Anthropic) argue benefits, @walden_yan argues risks (it is hard to coordinate). Need to be careful, but benefit in cases where independent decisions made by each sub-agent won't case conflicts.
10/ Cache context. @manusai mentions caching agent message history (system prompt, tool desc, past messages). Big cost / latency saving, but still does not get around long-context problems.
Still very early in all of this ..
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gwo7SF_asAA6sgn.jpg

linked_urls.title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance | Chroma
linked_urls.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically presumed to process context uniformly—that is, the model should handle the 10,000th token just as reliably as the 100th. However, in practice, this assumption does not hold. We observe that model performance varies significantly as input length changes, even on simple tasks. In this report, we evaluate 18 LLMs, including the state-of-the-art GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, and Qwen3 models. Our results reveal that models do not use their context uniformly; instead, their performance grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows.

After a year of “yet another agent framework,” this one feels genuinely refreshing.
@langchain just released a new Python package called deepagents, and I think it opens up some really interesting avenues.
It’s built around a simple idea: the best research and coding agents (Claude Code, Manus, etc.) all have a few things in common—
- a detailed system prompt
- a planning tool (even if it's a no-op)
- sub-agents for task decomposition
- Access to a file system for shared memory
deepagents packages those ideas into a framework you can tweak for your own use case.
Just `pip install deepagents` and you’re off.
Of course, it’s not for every use case.
But if you’re exploring long-horizon, vertical-specific agents, this is worth looking into.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
When using AI, there is a new term that has been floating around that expands well beyond "prompt engineering," and that is "context engineering."
While prompt engineering is foundational, context engineering takes it further by ensuring AI doesn't just follow instructions but operates with rich, relevant background to deliver precise results.
First, let's recap prompt engineering basics. When I coach teams in webinars, events, or client sessions, I always emphasize "RTO" as a simple framework:
🙋🏽‍♂️ Role: Assign a clear persona to the AI, like "You are an expert name analyzer" or "You are a sales development representative from XYZ company." This sets the tone and expertise level.
🛠️ Task: Break down the steps with markdown for clarity (e.g., numbered lists or bullets), and include guardrails like good/bad examples to prevent off-track outputs. For instance, show what a strong cold email looks like versus a generic one.
🤖 Output: Specify the exact format you want—JSON for structured data, bullet points for lists, or even a confidence score. This is crucial for token efficiency, especially in no-history platforms like @clayrun, where every prompt stands alone.
But context engineering goes beyond crafting that perfect prompt. As outlined in @langchain's excellent blog on "Context Engineering for Agents," it's about strategically filling the AI's "context window" (think of it as short-term memory) with the right info at each step to handle complex, multi-turn tasks without overload.
It includes:
📖 Instructions: Your core prompt (Prompt Engineering 101).
🧠 Knowledge: Feed in documents, websites, or use RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) with vector databases to reference real-time data—like pulling company intel for personalized sales outreach.
🛠️ Tools: Integrate agents or services like multi-tool chains (e.g., MCPs for custom workflows) to let AI call external APIs, automate steps in tools like @n8n_io.
Why does this matter?
AI models have limited context windows—much like human working memory. If I handed you a full book to read, how much would stick tomorrow? Overload the window, and outputs get fuzzy, leading to hallucinations or inaccuracies. In business production (e.g., outbound sales or data analysis), context engineering scales AI's capabilities, reduces costs, and boosts reliability by managing what gets prioritized.
KEY TAKEAWAYS:
Leverage reasoning models like ChatGPT's o3 or Grok 4 to refine prompts—ask follow-up questions or potential edge cases before running a full query. Then ask to output in a code snippet.
Add context: Query the AI on what tools/resources it needs (e.g., "What websites or examples would help?"), then provide them to ensure spot-on results.
Always define outputs clearly, and build in an "out"—instruct the AI to flag low-confidence responses (e.g., "If under 80% sure, say 'Insufficient data' and explain why") to avoid forced hallucinations.
Anything I'm missing that's worked well for you?

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
🏗️LangGraph now offers a durability mode for fine-grained persistence control.
Control how your agentic workflows resume (post crash, human intervention, timeout, you name it) with these 3 modes, from least to most durable:
⚡ "exit": fast (checkpoint only at end)
⚖️ "async": balanced (async during the next step)
🛡️ "sync": bulletproof (sync before each step)

Agentic Workflows using LangChain, Agentic Workflows & Function Calling
Why the focus on Agentic Workflows?
I used an AI research API to analyse emerging trends and identify those on the rise versus in decline.
Surprisingly, interest in AI Agents is waning, while two areas are surging:
- Advanced research and reasoning capabilities, and
- Agentic Workflows.
Agentic Workflows bridge the gap between traditional RPA
— which is often brittle, inflexible, and rigidly predetermined
— and full-fledged AI Agents, where the degree of autonomy can feel overwhelming.
Agentic Workflows strike an ideal balance:
They provide a foundational template for applications, enabling agency within defined boundaries, along with the adaptability and autonomy that traditional RPA sorely lacks.
Of course, all of this remains theoretical for me until I can implement it in the simplest form possible.
So, I discovered this excellent LangChain notebook that illustrates, in straightforward terms, how a few URLs are indexed in Chroma… and how the RAG lookup is configured as a function call.
This setup allows the LLM to introduce a layer of autonomy into the agentic workflow by deciding whether or not to invoke the RAG function.
You can easily envision extending this process to include multiple tools and functions at the disposal of the Agentic Workflow.
Personally, I believe function calling is under appreciated or not fully understood… but it’s truly an effective way to build resilience while maintaining a controlled level of agency.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
So @hwchase17 said “context engineering is becoming the most important skill an AI engineer can develop”...
He’s not wrong.
While this might be a bit inside baseball and I will definitely oversimplify things but bear with me as I’ve been wanting to write this post since I saw Harrison’s killer tweet on 06.23…so, finally, here we go.
Think of an LLM as a brain.
A brain without a body, arms, legs, hands etc isn’t capable of much. But a brain with all of those things?
It now has agency. It can accomplish things.
A brain inside a body could be thought of as a system of sorts.
Now think of an LLM as the brain that powers an intelligent system, the foundation which AI agents plug into and rely upon to accomplish those things.
An intelligent system where the left hand knows what the right hand is doing and so on and so forth.
But just like a human, an intelligent system’s brain, an LLM, needs to understand context to effectively guide the AI agents in their efforts to accomplish tasks.
Especially within increasingly complex circumstances, environments etc where nuance really matters.
💡 Without context, the intelligent system won’t be able to accomplish much. With context, you know the drill.
Just like that brain needs context to guide the body effectively, LLMs need rich context to accomplish tasks.
It’s a lot like when someone launches into a story without providing context and you aren’t really listening because all you can think about is when you can interrupt and ask them to back up and provide context…so that everything said afterwards makes sense and falls into place nicely.
💡 Without context, the story doesn’t land. With context, everything flows nicely.
Whereas prompt engineering is “focused on phrasing prompts cleverly to coax better answers…Context engineering is building dynamic systems to provide the right information and tools in the right format such that the LLM can plausibly accomplish the task.”
Why is this so important?
🏆 Building an Ontology Aware Intelligent System has competitive advantages written all over it…you know what I mean?

🌟Our latest LangChain Academy course – Deep Agents with LangGraph – is now live!🌟
Many agents today follow the same simple pattern: run in a loop, call tools. That architecture works well enough, but it breaks down as tasks get more complex.
Today, companies of all sizes – from startups to large enterprises – are building their own Deep Agents.
These agents dive deeper. They’re able to plan complex tasks and carry them out over longer time horizons.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
If a prototype takes a day, waiting a week for user feedback is "really painful," said Andrew Ng.
Well....now you can get user feedback in under 60 seconds :)
Whether you're prototyping a feature or building a full fledged product, learn how to build an AI-powered user research system that automatically generates user personas, conduct interviews, and synthesize insights. All in <60 seconds.
Includes a full code notebook, recorded tutorial, and docs.
The stack
🤖 @cerebras fast inference
🤖 @langchain's LangGraph for orchestrating multi-agent workflows
🤖 @langchain's LangSmith for tracing and evaluating
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1972725352276611073/img/yUNh_iiBaNzha5Nx.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1972725352276611073/vid/avc1/480x270/Z4u3tdR9j3jK7ger.mp4?tag=21
Quoting @AndrewYNg
The invention of modern writing instruments like the typewriter made writing easier, but they also led to the rise of writer’s block, where deciding what to write became the bottleneck. Similarly, the invention of agentic coding assistants has led to a new builder’s block, where the holdup is deciding what to build. I call this the Product Management Bottleneck.
Product management is the art and science of deciding what to build. Because highly agentic coding accelerates the writing of software to a given product specification, deciding what to build is the new bottleneck, especially in early-stage projects. As the teams I work with take advantage of agentic coders, I increasingly value product managers (PMs) who have very high user empathy and can make product decisions quickly, so the speed of product decision-making matches the speed of coding.
PMs with high user empathy can make decisions by gut and get them right a lot of the time. As new information comes in, they can keep refining their mental models of what users like or do not like — and thereby refine their gut — and keep making fast decisions of increasing quality.
Many tactics are available to get user feedback and other forms of data that shape our beliefs about users. They include conversations with a handful of users, focus groups, surveys, and A/B tests on scaled products. But to drive progress at GenAI speed, I find that synthesizing all these sources of data in a PM's gut helps us move faster.
Let me illustrate with an example. Recently, my team debated which of 4 features users would prefer. I had my instincts, but none of us were sure, so we surveyed about 1,000 users. The results contradicted my initial beliefs — I was wrong! So what was the right thing to do at this point?
- Option 1: Go by the survey and build what users told us clearly they prefer.
- Option 2: Examine the survey data in detail to see how it changes my beliefs about what users want. That is, refine my mental model of users. Then use my revised mental model to decide what to do.
Even though some would consider Option 1 the “data-driven” way to make decisions, I consider this an inferior approach for most projects. Surveys may be flawed. Further, taking time to run a survey before making a decision results in slow decision-making.
In contrast, using Option 2, the survey results give much more generalizable information that can help me shape not just this decision, but many others as well. And it lets me process this one piece of data alongside all the user conversations, surveys, market reports, and observations of user behavior when they’re engaging with our product to form a much fuller view on how to serve users. Ultimately, that mental model drives my product decisions.
Of course, this technique does not always scale. For example, with programmatic online advertising in which AI might try to optimize the number of clicks on ads shown, an automated system conducts far more experiments in parallel and gathers data on what users do and do not click on, to filter through a PM's mental model of users. When a system needs to make a huge number of decisions, such as what ads to show (or products to recommend) on a huge number of pages, PM review and human intuition do not scale.
But in products where a team is making a small number of critical decisions such as what key features to prioritize, I find that data — used to help build a good mental model of the user, which is then applied to make decisions very quickly — is still the best way to drive rapid progress and relieve the Product Management Bottleneck.

To celebrate the milestone, allow me to reflect on my journey and relationship with LC...
I don't have much experience w/ "vanilla" LangChain or the LC Python tools, but I've been an avid user of Deployments and the LangGraph TypeScript SDK for like a year now (started using Deployments back when it was still called "LangGraph Platform"). I think I might be one of the oldest users of both products.
TBH, my first impressions were mixed:
1- The Deployments product was very early/new and a bit rough around the edges (bad monorepo support, for example; some stability problems).
2- The LangGraph TypeScript SDK felt... not super TypeScript-y. (I get the sense they ported over a bunch of abstractions from the Python package).
But the benefits definitely outweighed the costs. In September 2024, Deployments + the LangGraph TypeScript SDK was one of the only ways that you could say FOR SURE that your agent was going to (a) work and (b) run smoothly in production.
(Also, their team worked hard as hell to ramp myself and my teammates up on agents. I was really won over by this and will forever be a LC stan as a result.)
(FWIW, I do use other agent frameworks and always try to remain unbiased / avoid shilling. But I also believe that customer support is "part of the product" - and LC is exceptional in this area.)
Over the past year, I've seen both Deployments and the TypeScript SDK evolve and mature significantly. Most of the problems I mentioned original problems have been addressed.
Still on my wishlist:
- Better monorepo support
- Better support for alternative runtimes/package managers (e.g. Bun, pnpm)
- Faster builds & deploys
- Slack notifications
In October 2025, I still feel that the overhead associated with building and hosting your own agent from scratch is too much for most teams to take on, even at large companies. In particular, first-class support for streaming is massive; this seems like it would be a huge PITA to build in-house. I'm happy to let LangChain take care of all of this for me.
Overall, I've been very impressed at LC's ability to iterate and absorb feedback, especially when some of it has not been delivered in the... kindest way. They're a very humble and hardworking team.
Glad to see them winning!

Major day with major versions for the LangChain community! We're 1.0 for both LangChain and LangGraph.
LangChain was rebuilt from the ground up -- to be way more streamlined, more flexible, and more powerful. Just so much better in every way. This was not an easy call to rewrite a framework that is already so ubiquitous.
LangChain is now centered around a tool-calling in a loop agent architecture, with model agnosticism as a core benefit.
What's changed:
- better content blocks to standardize across models
- fewer agent options, only ones that have our stamp of approval
- a new concept (middleware) that helps with controllability and context engineering
- runs on LangGraph runtime (more durable, better for human-in-the-loop + stateful interactions)

New Conceptual Guide: You don’t know what your agent will do until it’s in production 👀
With traditional software, you ship with reasonable confidence. Test coverage handles most paths. Monitoring catches errors, latency, and query issues. When something breaks, you read the stack trace.
Agents are different. Natural language input is unbounded. LLMs are sensitive to subtle prompt variations. Multi-step reasoning chains are hard to anticipate in dev.
Production monitoring for agents needs a different playbook. In our latest conceptual guide, we cover why agent observability is a different problem, what to actually monitor, and what we've learned from teams deploying agents at scale.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
I think this is a likely evolution. For sure building agentic software using Claude Agents SDK or DeepAgents SDK really works well.
And there's clearly a compounding effect if you are able to manifest learnings of your agent sessions into context that is useful to the agent on the next run.
There are many ways to slice the onion here, but I think self-updatable software in many verticals which automatically captures some essence of user preferences is going to happen for sure.
In fact all the building blocks are there such that it can exist already - I think we just don't have an 'aligned set of recipes / patterns' that are established and used consistently by software teams. But we'll probably get there soon, and honestly there is a TON of opportunity here to figure out the right ways to do it.
Systems like Claude Code / Deep Agents / Claude Agents SDK are just a set of legos. So many ways to put it together.
Quoting @t_blom
Pretty soon, I think we’ll see software shipping with Claude Code SDK embedded inside.
Users will use it to configure and modify the software to meet their exact needs.
The best changes will get passed back to the software developer and reincorporated in the master release.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
virtual filesystems!
filesystems are such a great agent pattern, we lean into it pretty heavily at LangChain for data storage, memory, collaboration scratchpad between agents, more
a lot of storage can “look like a filesystem” if you map fs-ops like read, write, ls to a “backend” like S3 or Notion or Box or your own custom rolled one
The benefit is that agents get an interface to plug into existing storage platforms without copying data + stay in their training distribution of being great at fs-ops because they still see “read, write…”
Mounting S3 was something we did a ton at AWS to expose large data for model training on SageMaker, the pattern works really well for agents too
Quoting @ClementDelangue
Local AI is free, fast & secure!
So today we're introducing hf-mount: attach any storage bucket, model or dataset from @huggingface as a local filesystem.
This is a game changer, as it allows you to attach remote storage that is 100x bigger than your local machine's disk. This is also perfect for Agentic storage!!
Let's go!

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
thinking through the implementation details of read_file is a great mental exercise on harness+context eng
the magical experience of being able to read any file means answering questions like:
- how should we handle large files that could blow up context
- how do we prompt and eval agents to use correct line offsets in files
- how do we handle pathological cases like very long lines in files?
- what does it even mean to support reading a pdf? how do we parse it and what/how much do we inject on each read?
- images are all different sizes, should we standardize the resize operation? how does that affect perception tasks?
- are there cases when agents should just use bash to read files? what are those and how do we prompt that behavior
lots of fun engineering and debugging in simple harness primitives
many design decisions in making an agent product feel simple & smooth even if there’s a lot of code underlying it
we want to make that easy with deepagents :)
Quoting @hwchase17
Another gem in deepagents 0.5 - read file now supports a bunch of file types!

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
nice thread, love this line of thinking about intelligence systems though I disagree in some ways. Current thoughts which will probably adapt!:
1. “humans don’t have a harness”
we totally do. the ability to create and use external tools and our bodies is one of the main reasons we’re so effective at operating in our environment
A harness is the interface that allows a model to efficiently operate in the world
Our bodies are the natural analog to a harness, eyes to perceive the world a certain way, hands with particular dexterity
But it extends to things like a knife to cut things, a calculator to compute things, binoculars to see things far away are completely external to me and incredibly Task dependent. but if i need to do that Task well and I don’t have those tools in “my harness”, I’m going to practically be terrible at those tasks
for humans the boundary between us and our harness isn’t super clear to me. but for any AI system to do effective work, it will need a harness - this is how it even interacts with the external world
But it may be that AGI is smart enough to bootstrap one just-in-time which is an exciting avenue of research
2. is it necessary to separate client vs server side tools to talk about general intelligence?
I like the framing that certain “tools” are practically so useful (computer tools, instructions to invoke behavior) that it makes sense to train models alongside them! so labs close them behind APIs.
but idt that makes the hidden feature a contributor to general intelligence, it’s just useful for economically valuable tasks today.
intelligence in the “learning to solve a new task” sense is different and not always correlated to what goes behind a server. The web search tool summarizing context for the model is a decent example.
3. A big chunk of harnesses will fall away with better models
I bet this is true, it will be a good thing! Harnesses primitives like context injection to force models to self-verify work or continue working ideally should occur in the model layer
Again I think the most exciting area is models that have a base set of primitives that just-in-time assemble their harness to complete any task.
again the Arc Project and this line of research are incredibly important, we should all spend a ton of time and compute on this, my thoughts will probably evolve on it :)
Quoting @mikeknoop
LLM systems swallow harness progress.
The most general/universal LLM innovations migrate from client-side harnesses to server-side tools.
Innovation typically happens first inside the harness.
For example, AI reasoning was originally a harness around GPT-3 ("let's think step by step"). This approach worked so well that it migrated behind the API as a tool (competitive reasons were also a factor; but general utility dominated).
Many wouldn't think of AI reasoning as a tool but it definitely is (it's a tool to do natural language program synthesis -- but that's another topic). The same happened with code interpreter which started out as a client-side harness and moved server-side.
These tools are made available at inference time to the model alongside specific training to teach the model when and how to use each tool. Because of this, the line between tool and model can get quite blurry. Best to consider such tools as "internal" to the LLM system.
This is actually a good test of how general a harness feature is. If a feature remains "stuck" client-side, say inside codex or claude code, then it's likely very task- or domain- specific.
Client-side harnesses typically encode a lot of human G factor for specific domains. Whereas tools, due to usage pressure of frontier LLMs, are required to be as general as possible else they wouldn't make the cut.
So if you care about measuring AGI it's a good idea to pay attention to default LLM system capabilities behind high usage LLM APIs.
And if you care about bleeding edge research ideas, such as RLMs, it's a good idea to pay attention to harness innovation.
Ultimately, AGI will not depend on a harness in the same sense humans don't depend on a harness.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
summary:
Great post from @Vtrivedy10 and other folks at @langchain on building evals for agents. Some concept I really liked:
- Self-documenting them with docstrings and adding tags, so that you can selectively run them
- Be thoughtful around a 'taxonomy' of evals. What is a logical grouping for them that applies to your domain?
- 'Correctness' might have multiple dimensions. Figure out what these dimensions are for your domain, and then test to those dimensions.
- Capture traces systematically, and then use an agent on these trades (e.g Claude Code) to analyze the traces for potential evals you should be building.
Also, this from the 'what's next' section:
"Evals as a mechanism to auto-improve agents for tasks in real time"
This is something that I've been thinking about a lot, and implementing in a few different ways in my systems. I don't have a perfect pattern for this, but I think it's definitely working -- and this is clearly going to be the future here
Quoting @Vtrivedy10
