clean_title: Open Model mission to enable cost-effective world-class agents
summary:
we're on an Open Model mission to help builders create world class agents >20x cheaper than what they have today
a couple things have become evident recently:
1. The age of the token subsidy is being pulled back
2. Open Models have crossed an intelligence threshold making them viable for real world agents at a fraction of the cost
As teams get exponentially larger monthly bills from the labs, it's worth exploring how many agents today perform just as well using Open Models
Check out the numbers on external evals + try it yourself by dogfooding and running on internal evals - @OpenRouter and @ArtificialAnlys have great leaderboards and breakdowns of what people are using. The time investment is definitely worth the massive cost savings
- Instead of Sonnet 4.6 (or even 5.5/Opus) try Kimi-2.6, GLM5.1, Deepseek v4 pro, etc
- Instead of Haiku try DeepSeekv4 Flash, Nemotron, etc
Open models require some tuning to make sure they work well in your harness for your task (another reason why open harnesses are important)
The closed models are excellent, there's no need to full-scale rip them out. Often the first use of Open Models is as subagents or using a closed frontier model as an Advisor to an open driver model
At LangChain we want to make it as easy as possible to build the best agents in the world as cheaply and quickly as possible. We're leaning into open models heavily across our products and libraries
try out an open model in deepagents in just a couple lines and come ride the open model, open harness future

Harrison Chase discusses an open model initiative aimed at helping builders create high-quality agents at over 20 times lower cost than current solutions. Recent trends show that the era of token subsidies is ending, and open models have reached an intelligence level making them suitable for real-world applications with significantly reduced expenses.

He highlights that many teams can achieve comparable performance using open models like Kimi-2.6, GLM5.1, and DeepSeek v4 Pro instead of more expensive closed models such as Sonnet or Haiku. title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Real-time responsiveness in production agents via streaming and concurrency control
summary:
production agents need to feel responsive in real time. two primitives make that possible: streaming and concurrent request control.
on streaming: streaming is a first-class primitive in LangSmith's agent server. partial output flows to the client as the agent produces it: token by token, step by step, or as custom application events.
on concurrency: in a live session, users don't wait politely for a response before sending the next message. we call this double-texting, and your runtime needs an explicit position on what to do:
1. enqueue: finish the current run, process the new message after. safe default.
2. reject: block new input until the current run finishes.
3. interrupt: halt mid-run, preserve state, resume with the new input. right when the second message builds on the first.
4. rollback: halt mid-run, revert all progress, start fresh. right when the second message replaces the first.
concurrent request docs:
full breakdown of the runtime:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHffW-QXYAAWTNg.png
clean_summary:
Production agents need to feel responsive in real time. Two key primitives enable this: streaming and concurrent request control.

Streaming is a first-class feature in LangSmith's agent server, allowing partial outputs to flow to the client as the agent produces them, whether token by token, step by step, or through custom events.

For concurrency, in a live session, users can send multiple messages without waiting for responses. This is called double-texting, and the runtime must decide how to handle new input: enqueue (finish current run, then process), reject (block until current finishes), interrupt (pause, preserve state, and resume with new input), or rollback (abort current, revert progress, and start fresh). A full breakdown of the runtime is available in the linked documentation.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Conflicting views on proprietary RL’d vs open harnesses and model generalization
summary:
There’s a bunch of conflicting stances I don’t fully understand in the debate of Proprietary RL’d vs Open Harness, Model intelligence, and Agent Labs building harnesses for bespoke tasks
Not all of the below can be true:
1. Model is post-trained with a harness in the loop so it rocks with those tools, instruction styles ✅ i’m largely on board, makes sense, up to an extent…
2. But Agent Labs have been and continue to outperform native harnesses across many economically valuable tasks like long horizon coding using the same models…so what gives? This is partly definitely leaning heavily into the “Task” part of Model-Harness-Task fit. Are they just largely copying the default harness?
3. As we add custom instructions, tools, skills, how quickly am I going to ”out of distribution”? What does out of distribution even mean? Is it just I need to follow the tool spec and some basic instruction language?
If I clone the Codex or Claude Code harness in Pi or LangChain and start tweaking it, I’m pretty sure perf will be fine for most tasks and will probably improve for tasks I extend it for.
There’s no general purpose harness right? Everything is task specific? All that seems to matter is setting up a good way to pipe context to the model for that task. I feel like having a good base (Pi of LangChain create_agent) and building a good tool and context stack on top of this for an agent works for people!
4. “Models are approaching AGI level intelligence and can generalize to very difficult out of distribution tasks”
so how much does the natively post-trained harness matter here? Model has THAT much trouble generalizing? And also see point 2 above where a careful designer seems to overcome this?
5. Frontier labs are making edits to their harness that cause degradations in behavior that they can’t measure for months? So how good is everyone’s base harness really? It seems like we’re all just empirically experimenting on harnesses and that’s fine, but the vibes from the labs building harnesses feels different even if numbers don’t reflect this.
there’s definitely more things here I’d love to understand people’s views on. And note: it’s def in my personal interest for it to be true that Well-Built Open Harnesses are better practically and performance wise. So would love to hear the total opposite side to see why others disagree and why
I can probably answer some of the above conflicts myself but not everything above can hold in all cases
clean_summary:
There are several conflicting perspectives in the debate over proprietary reinforcement learning harnesses versus open-source ones, especially regarding model intelligence and agent labs building task-specific harnesses. Some believe that post-training models with a harness in the loop perform well with instruction styles, but others point out that agent labs often outperform native harnesses on valuable tasks like long-horizon coding, raising questions about task-specificity and generalization.

Adding custom instructions and tools may lead to out-of-distribution issues, but tweaking existing harnesses like Codex or Claude Code might still maintain or improve performance for extended tasks. The idea that models are approaching AGI-level intelligence and can handle difficult out-of-distribution tasks depends heavily on how well the harness and task design are managed. Some labs make unmeasured modifications to their harnesses that degrade behavior over time, suggesting that the quality of base harnesses varies and that empirical experimentation is ongoing.

Overall, there is curiosity about whether well-built open harnesses could outperform proprietary ones in practice and performance, and a desire to understand the reasons behind differing views in this debate.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Open-weight LLMs on agent tasks and the importance of interfaces
summary:
open-weight LLMs have come a long way on agent tasks! but the harness you wrap them in matters just as much as the model itself, and arguably the interface you use to drive that harness matters even more.
dev workflows are deeply personal. what works well for one developer may hinder another, so it's difficult to converge on a single UX that isn't either compromising or too generalized (e.g. CLI vs. TUI vs. GUI vs. IDE extension)
while it doesn't come without drawbacks, ACP a solid stopgap for running the same harness across multiple interfaces. pick your frontend, keep your agent.
deepagents ships with this out of the box -- two ways to plug it in:
- deepagents-acp is our standalone ACP server to serve *any* agent
- `deepagents-cli --acp` to use our existing CLI agent over ACP
point any ACP-compatible client at it and you've got the same deepagents harness, your choice of open-weight model & provider, and your choice of interface.
some popular exemplars:
- `toad` is an agent-agnostic TUI that ships deepagents support built-in, made possible via ACP (@willmcgugan @textualizeio)
- you can use deepagents directly in any modern IDE, see this blog post from @jetbrains coauthored by our very own @Hacubu:
the model is yours to pick. the interface is yours to pick. the harness shouldn't be the thing that locks you in.
clean_summary:
Open-weight large language models have advanced significantly in agent tasks. However, the interface used to wrap and drive these models is equally important, as it affects developer workflows, which are highly personal and vary between CLI, TUI, GUI, and IDE extensions.

ACP (Agent Control Protocol) offers a practical way to run the same harness across multiple interfaces, allowing developers to keep their preferred frontend while maintaining flexibility in model choice and provider. Deepagents provides out-of-the-box support for ACP, with a standalone server and CLI options, enabling consistent harnessing regardless of the interface.

Examples include 'toad', a terminal-based agent-agnostic TUI with deepagents support, and integration with modern IDEs, as highlighted in a JetBrains blog post coauthored by @Hacubu. The key message is that the model and interface are flexible; the harness should not be restrictive.

Examples include `toad`, a TUI agent-agnostic interface with built-in deepagents support, and integration with modern IDEs, as discussed in a JetBrains blog post coauthored by @Hacubu. The model and interface are flexible; the harness should not limit your choices.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Agent harness evolution along temporal and lateral axes
summary:
It feels like agent harness evolution runs on two axes that usually get conflated.
There’s the temporal axis: simplify as models improve, stripping components that compensated for limitations the new model no longer has. Sonnet 4.5 needed context resets; opus 4.5 didn’t. Opus 4.5 needed sprint decomposition for planning; opus 4.6 didn’t.
Then there’s the lateral axis: tune the harness per model family, because different models need different tool names, prompt framing, middleware, and orchestration at any given point in time.
Model labs mostly see the temporal axis because their harness only talks to one model family. But if you’re building in a multi-model world with models from anthropic today, openai tomorrow, google next week, and an OS lab after that, you probably should care about both.
Harness profiles are a mechanism for that second axis, they allow you to keep the agent abstraction stable, but let the model-specific harness contents move.
clean_summary:
Agent harness evolution occurs along two axes that are often conflated. The first is the temporal axis: as models improve, components that compensated for previous limitations are removed, such as context resets or planning decompositions. The second is the lateral axis: tuning the harness for different model families, since each may require different tool names, prompt framing, middleware, and orchestration.

Most labs focus on the temporal axis because their harnesses only interact with one model family. However, in a multi-model environment involving models from different providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, or others, it is important to consider both axes. Harness profiles enable this by maintaining a stable agent abstraction while allowing model-specific harness contents to change.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Agent and harness engineering: opinions on customization, evaluation, and the future of task-specific AI
summary:
Strong Opinions, Loosely Held on Agent + Harness Engineering:
1. You can outperform any default harness+model (including codex & claude code) on pretty much any Task by engineering the harness around it. Using the exact same model, curate prompts, tools, skills, hooks for that Task. This harness optimization process is becoming much more agent driven with humans reviewing and curating evals/rewards to hill climb on. “Just say what you want”.
2. A “general purpose” agent/harness doesn’t really exist, it’s a tradeoff between time spent on customizing the agent and performance (cost, latency, accuracy) on a Task. I don’t exactly follow what a general purpose means tbh. Who decides what’s general and what’s not?
3. But if the “general purpose” agent/harness existed, it would look like a good coding agent
4. Building a Task specific harness will most likely converge to good prompt & tool design (probably packaged up as a Skill) as models become smarter and better at in-context learning
5. Evals are a moat and thus data to produce evals is a moat. Especially true for vertical agent companies. This is because agents can fit to most Eval sets today. If Evals measurably encode all the good behavior your agent needs to do, then this signal can be hill climbed to improve your agent
6. Frontier closed models are far too expensive for the large majority of tasks the world needs to do. As teams start mapping costs to ROI, Open Model Harness Engineering will take off even more. It is almost always worth the investment to at least try to get a potential 20x+ cost reduction
7. A large chunk of design decisions around Task decomposition and context engineering exist solely because our usable context window is 50-100k. Agents that become excellent at breaking down tasks, applying compaction appropriately, and orchestrating subagents as sub-task workers will be the most delightful products to do real work.
8. We’re entering an Age of Unbundled (& Rebundled) Agents where Subagents exposed as Tools do a ton of domain specific work on behalf of an orchestrator agent. The Harness becomes a box that gets populated with the exact set of tools, skills, and subagents needed to solve that task or sub-task.
Examples include WarpGrep (search), Chroma Context-1 (search), Nemotron 3 Omni (small multimodal), etc. Bespoke agents that rock at narrow tasks orchestrated as tools.
This also applies to software as tools that are used by agents via Skills like Remotion or Blender. Different harnesses bundle together the tooling needed to complete that narrow task.
End of opinions, these may change by the time this tweet goes out or may double down and expand on these in an article
clean_summary:
Strong opinions on agent and harness engineering emphasize that outperforming default models like Codex and Claude Code on specific tasks is best achieved by designing custom harnesses that include curated prompts, tools, and skills. This process is becoming more agent-driven, with humans reviewing and optimizing evaluations and rewards. The idea of a truly general-purpose agent or harness is questioned, as performance depends on the tradeoff between customization effort and task performance. If such a general-purpose system existed, it would resemble a capable coding agent.

Building task-specific harnesses is likely to lead to better prompt and tool design, often packaged as skills, as models improve at in-context learning. Evaluation data and sets are a competitive moat, especially for vertical companies, since agents can fit most evals today, and good evals encode the desired behaviors for hill climbing. Cost considerations also matter, with open model harness engineering offering a potential 20x+ cost reduction, making it a worthwhile investment.

With large context windows of 50-100k tokens, agents that can decompose tasks, apply compression, and orchestrate subagents will be highly effective. We are entering an era of unbundled and rebundled agents, where subagents or tools—such as search engines or domain-specific multimodal models—are integrated as needed. This approach extends to software tools used via skills, enabling narrow, domain-specific tasks to be handled efficiently by bespoke agents.

clean_title: LangGraph introduces delta channels for efficient checkpointing
summary:
one of the features i'm most excited about in our upcoming langgraph release is delta channels!
the langgraph runtime lets you "checkpoint" agent progress at every step (model call, tool call, hooks). the problem, though, is that checkpoints bloat quickly when context is long!
delta channel mitigates this with diff based storage from checkpoint to checkpoint. with delta channels, you still have a full history of agent progress, the only diff (haha get it) is the storage format.
in-depth blog coming soon, but in the meantime, try it out and lmk what you think!
clean_summary: One of the features I'm most excited about in our upcoming LangGraph release is delta channels. The LangGraph runtime allows you to checkpoint agent progress at every step, such as model calls, tool calls, and hooks. However, checkpoints can quickly bloat when the context is long. Delta channels address this by using diff-based storage from checkpoint to checkpoint, maintaining a full history of agent progress while reducing storage size. An in-depth blog is coming soon, but in the meantime, try it out and share your feedback.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Open models enable cost-effective agentic batch processing
summary:
Open Models Make Agentic Batch Processing Economically Viable
A lot of world’s work looks like “Do X for EVERY Y”
- read every trace
- respond to every email
- deep dive into every document
- enrich every lead
This is the domain of Agentic Batch Computing
Much of the world’s work does not need peak frontier intelligence, it needs carefully shaped intelligence pointed at specific tasks
The holy grail here is having a tailored agent run on every single one of these data points + tasks
The world is producing more data than ever before. To understand and process it at scale, we’re going to have to point Intelligence and Compute at this
Open Models are a fantastic tool here
- they’re often an order of magnitude cheaper
- they can be finetuned (SFT & RL) to fit to your exact task distribution and outperform frontier models for your task
As companies contend with rising AI costs, Open Models and specialized models become incredibly important to make sure there’s good ROI on AI spend
here to help as you let the token machine rip without busting the bank (and with better results) 🫡
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHvF1cbXQAgmJIR.jpg
clean_summary:
A lot of work involves doing the same task for every data point, such as reading traces, responding to emails, or analyzing documents. This is where agentic batch computing comes in, focusing intelligence on specific tasks rather than peak frontier performance.

The goal is to have tailored agents run on each data point and task. With the increasing volume of data, using open models becomes valuable because they are often much cheaper and can be fine-tuned through supervised and reinforcement learning to outperform larger, more expensive models for particular tasks.

As AI costs rise, open models and specialized variants are crucial for maintaining good return on investment. They help process data at scale without breaking the bank, while delivering better results.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Sandboxes enable code execution in deep agents for complex problem solving
summary:
this is the part of the deep agents production series i've been most excited to get to: sandboxes
without an execution environment, a production agent is only as capable as its fixed toolset.
give an agent an execution environment where it can write and run code, and you give it a general-purpose toolkit for approaching complex and diverse problems. that's what sandboxes unlock.
think data analysis: an agent that can write and execute its own queries, process the results, and generate a report is fundamentally more useful than one that can only call a predefined analysis tools.
deep agents handles this through sandbox backends. configure one and the agent gets an execute tool scoped to that environment. no backend, no tool. deep agents is provider-agnostic: daytona, modal, runloop, and langsmith sandboxes all supported, swappable with a config change.
secure code execution requires isolation: code running on your host can read env vars, exfiltrate api keys, cause real damage. but the sandbox protects your host, not the sandbox itself. credentials placed inside are still reachable via prompt injection. the auth proxy pattern addresses this: credentials live in workspace secrets, get injected on outbound requests by a sidecar, and never land inside the execution environment.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHvNcytXwAwVzFl.png
clean_summary:
This part of the deep agents production series focuses on sandboxes. Without an execution environment, a production agent is limited to its fixed toolset. Providing an agent with a sandbox where it can write and run code unlocks the ability to approach complex and diverse problems, such as data analysis tasks that involve writing and executing queries, processing results, and generating reports.

Deep agents supports sandbox backends that can be configured to give the agent an execute tool scoped to that environment. The system is provider-agnostic, supporting platforms like Daytona, Modal, Runloop, and LangSmith, which can be swapped with a simple configuration change. Secure code execution requires isolation to prevent malicious code from causing harm or exfiltrating secrets. Credentials stored as workspace secrets are injected into outbound requests via a sidecar, ensuring they do not land inside the execution environment, addressing the risks of prompt injection.

BYO sandbox with deepagents!
Quoting @sydneyrunkle
this is the part of the deep agents production series i've been most excited to get to: sandboxes
without an execution environment, a production agent is only as capable as its fixed toolset.
give an agent an execution environment where it can write and run code, and you give it a general-purpose toolkit for approaching complex and diverse problems. that's what sandboxes unlock.
think data analysis: an agent that can write and execute its own queries, process the results, and generate a report is fundamentally more useful than one that can only call a predefined analysis tools.
deep agents handles this through sandbox backends. configure one and the agent gets an execute tool scoped to that environment. no backend, no tool. deep agents is provider-agnostic: daytona, modal, runloop, and langsmith sandboxes all supported, swappable with a config change.
secure code execution requires isolation: code running on your host can read env vars, exfiltrate api keys, cause real damage. but the sandbox protects your host, not the sandbox itself. credentials placed inside are still reachable via prompt injection. the auth proxy pattern addresses this: credentials live in workspace secrets, get injected on outbound requests by a sidecar, and never land inside the execution environment.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHvNcytXwAwVzFl.png
clean_summary: Deep agents can be equipped with sandboxes, which provide execution environments where they can write and run code. This capability allows agents to handle complex tasks like data analysis more effectively by executing queries, processing results, and generating reports. Deep agents supports multiple sandbox backends, such as Daytona, Modal, Runloop, and LangSmith, which are interchangeable via configuration. Secure code execution is achieved through isolation and the use of an auth proxy pattern, ensuring credentials remain protected inside workspace secrets while preventing prompt injection attacks.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Observability and time travel in deep agent deployment with LangSmith
summary:
concluding my "taking deep agents to production" series with arguably the most important component: observability.
when you deploy a deep agent with LangSmith, you automatically get traces for every run: a full record of every LLM call, tool call, and middleware hook. for long-running agents, you can use agents like Polly, the LangSmith assistant, to reason over long traces and identify where a trajectory went wrong. traces are observational: they tell you what happened.
time travel is experimental. built into the deep agent runtime, it's how you explore what an agent trajectory would look like if the agent had different context at some point. pick any checkpoint in a run's history, modify the state, and resume. the fork runs forward as its own branch, the original stays intact, and the full agent loop re-triggers.
the combination of traces and time travel is powerful for the agent improvement cycle!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HH0Asp5XAAUTS52.png
clean_summary:
Harrison Chase concludes his series on taking deep agents to production by highlighting the importance of observability. Using LangSmith, deploying a deep agent automatically provides traces for every run, recording all LLM calls, tool calls, and middleware hooks, which help understand what happened during execution.

For long-running agents, tools like Polly enable reasoning over extended traces to identify issues. Traces are observational, showing exactly what occurred. The concept of time travel is built into the deep agent runtime, allowing exploration of alternative trajectories by modifying the agent's state at any checkpoint and resuming from there. This combination of traces and time travel creates a powerful feedback loop for improving agent performance.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: The importance of measurement and iteration in agent development
summary:
my fave point from here: the earlier you think about your agent as a system that can be measured & improved, the faster you can get a robust agent into production
This isn’t just a technical thing, it’s a human & team thing. Teams that succeed here ask questions like:
- “what do I need my agent to do to make our customers happy?”
- “What scenarios will my agent encounter in the wild and how can we recreate that in our testing”
Evals are the substrate that determines what your agent does in production. They’re training data for agents because we literally fit our agent to pass Evals via hill-climbing algorithms and human edits to pass failure modes
Once you get your agent into users hands, the eval generation loop compounds. Production data uncovers more issues, these issues turn into Evals, and the agent fits to improve over more cases that could not be captured without real user data.
In the early stages, teams dogfooding their product becomes the feedback signal
Curating evals and running experiments on different agent variants is a muscle every team develops, our goal is to create tooling so every team can create the best agents for their tasks using this foundation
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HH5OQfcXEAQjevD.jpg
Quoting @hwchase17
clean_summary:
My favorite point from here is that the earlier you think of your agent as a system that can be measured and improved, the faster you can deploy a robust agent into production. This approach is not just technical but also human and team-oriented. Successful teams ask questions like what their agent needs to do to satisfy customers and how to recreate real-world scenarios in testing.

Evaluations serve as the foundation for guiding agent behavior in production. They act as training data, allowing agents to pass through hill-climbing algorithms and human edits to handle failure modes. Once an agent is in users' hands, the feedback loop intensifies: real user data reveals issues, which become new evaluations, leading to further improvements. Early on, teams rely on internal testing as a feedback signal.

Developing the skill to curate evaluations and experiment with different agent variants is crucial. The goal is to create tools so every team can build the best agents for their specific tasks using this iterative foundation.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Improving agent deployment with better testing, tracing, and feedback
summary:
> shipped the agent
> opened the dashboard
> latency: fine
> error rate: fine
> users: unhappy
> checked the responses
> technically correct
> wrong tool called 3 steps earlier
> no trace to follow
> no dataset to reproduce it
> no eval to catch it next time
> this wasn't a model problem
> it was an ops problem
> build, test, deploy, monitor - in that order
> skip test: you deploy guesses
> skip monitor: you lose the signal
> skip the loop: every version starts from zero
the fix:
> small eval dataset before production
> traces capturing the full agent trajectory
> LLM-as-judge scoring tool calls and policy
> feedback attached to the exact run that broke
> shared infra so every team doesn't rebuild this

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Thoughts on synthetic data generation for evaluation and environment building
summary:
thoughts after doing a bunch of synthetic data gen for eval + environment building
- LLMs are incredible projections of the world bundled into a set of weights
- but doing targeted extraction of certain distributions from those weight is incredibly difficult to do at scale. this is especially true for distributions that are less represented in the training corpus like long sequences of data
- rubric design + tons of compute on data generation and more importantly validation is a good recipe that can help you build datasets beyond the natural tendencies of models today. these are things like programattic tests on length, verifiers running with ground truth, and judges evaluating each stage of generation
- synthetic data design can be framed as an ultra long horizon agentic task. this is helpful framing because it lets us use the most powerful tools we have today…coding agents
- it’s unclear to me the exact deviations between frontier models for large scale synthetic data production. anecdotally Opus seemed to follow diversity stipulations better but it’s unclear how this holds at scale
- the ideal scenario is distilling the verification, instruction following, and diversity primitives into frontier open models where token costs are 20x less
- it’s better to have 3 good examples than 50 that are hard to understand
will be doing a lot more of this! it’s actually very fun and required at scale to test many types of agents
clean_summary:
Harrison Chase reflects on using synthetic data to evaluate and build environments for language models. He notes that while LLMs are impressive projections of the world encoded in weights, extracting specific distributions, especially for less-represented data like long sequences, is very challenging at scale.

He advocates for careful rubric design, extensive data generation, and validation processes, such as programmatic tests, verifiers with ground truth, and judges for evaluation, to create datasets that go beyond models' natural tendencies. Framing synthetic data creation as an ultra-long horizon agentic task allows leveraging coding agents, which are among the most powerful tools available today.

Chase observes that different frontier models may vary in how well they produce diverse synthetic data, with anecdotal evidence suggesting Opus follows diversity rules better, though scale effects are unclear. The goal is to distill verification, instruction following, and diversity into open models with much lower token costs. He emphasizes that having a few clear, high-quality examples is better than many confusing ones and plans to continue exploring this approach, as it is both fun and essential for testing many agent types at scale.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Nebius partners with LangChain to integrate Token Factory for AI agents
summary:
$NBIS announced a partnership with LangChain to integrate Nebius Token Factory with LangChain’s Deep Agents.
The goal is to make it easier for teams building AI agents on LangChain to run those workloads on Nebius infrastructure using open-source models.
The integration combines:
• LangChain Deep Agents for orchestration
• LangSmith for tracing and evaluation
• Nebius Token Factory as the inference backend
• Tavily for real-time web search and content extraction
This matters because agentic workflows usually require more infrastructure than simple chatbot interactions. A single agent workflow can involve planning, sub-agent calls, tool use, memory retrieval, retries, and multiple inference requests.
Nebius Token Factory supports 30+ open-source models, including Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, and NVIDIA Nemotron. It also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, dedicated endpoints, autoscaling, and a 99.9% uptime SLA.
One useful part of the integration is that teams can route different sub-agents to different models. For example, they can use a larger model for planning, a faster model for execution, and a lighter model for tool-calling. This can help optimize cost and performance across the agent workflow.
The integration also supports embeddings and semantic retrieval through the langchain-nebius package, meaning teams can run more of the agent pipeline on Nebius infrastructure.
Overall, this is another step in Nebius positioning Token Factory as infrastructure for production AI workloads, especially for teams that want to build agents using open models.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: SmithDB: a data layer optimized for agent observability workloads
summary:
"Industry-leading performance across every key observability workload" 🚀
Agent traces are nested, long-running, and full of large payloads. Making them searchable and interactive needs a data layer designed for that shape
SmithDB is that data layer.
Quoting @ankush_gola11
We built SmithDB: the database purpose built for agent observability workloads that now powers many parts of LangSmith.
Agent observability presents a challenging data problem. Agent traces can contain tens of thousands of intermediate spans and large, unbounded payloads. These characteristics are a direct result of agents running for longer time horizons and LLM context window sizes growing.
Traditional data infrastructure was not built to handle the complexities associated with storing and querying this data.
SmithDB brings LangSmith up to 12x performance improvements across access patterns most important for agent observability. I’ve been working on SmithDB directly with an amazing team over the past few months, and I’m incredibly proud of the results we’re seeing.
I wrote a bit more about the story and engineering challenges behind SmithDB in this blog.
Additionally, if you’re a systems engineer interested in building the future of agent observability, please reach out!
clean_summary:
Agent traces are nested, long-running, and contain large payloads, making them difficult to search and interact with using traditional data infrastructure. SmithDB is a purpose-built database designed to handle these complexities.

SmithDB now powers many parts of LangSmith and delivers up to 12 times performance improvements across key access patterns for agent observability. The development involved overcoming engineering challenges related to storing and querying extensive trace data, especially as agent run times and LLM context sizes grow. The work is documented in a blog, and system engineers interested in advancing agent observability are encouraged to reach out.

Huge work from @ankush_gola11 and team
Quoting @ankush_gola11
We built SmithDB: the database purpose built for agent observability workloads that now powers many parts of LangSmith.
Agent observability presents a challenging data problem. Agent traces can contain tens of thousands of intermediate spans and large, unbounded payloads. These characteristics are a direct result of agents running for longer time horizons and LLM context window sizes growing.
Traditional data infrastructure was not built to handle the complexities associated with storing and querying this data.
SmithDB brings LangSmith up to 12x performance improvements across access patterns most important for agent observability. I’ve been working on SmithDB directly with an amazing team over the past few months, and I’m incredibly proud of the results we’re seeing.
I wrote a bit more about the story and engineering challenges behind SmithDB in this blog.
Additionally, if you’re a systems engineer interested in building the future of agent observability, please reach out!
clean_summary: SmithDB is a new database designed specifically for agent observability workloads, addressing the challenge of storing and querying complex trace data with many intermediate spans and large payloads. Traditional infrastructure was not suited for this task, but SmithDB achieves up to 12 times performance improvements across key access patterns. The development involved a dedicated team working over several months, with further details available in a blog post. The system aims to support the growing complexity of agent data as LLMs and long-horizon agents become more prevalent.

clean_title: Engine: a tool for improving agents by connecting traces to fixes and evals
summary:
Agent observability is a means to an end: making your agent better.
But observability and evals tools have traditionally failed to connect traces to meaningful actions. Agent engineering teams are left combing through traces, guessing at root causes, and writing evals manually.
We built Engine to close the agent improvement loop. Engine monitors your agent's traces, creates ready-to-merge fixes, and writes evals.
Now every trace becomes a fix, an eval, and a better agent.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2054941354762080256/img/vqjyy9mwAQ0eab12.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2054941354762080256/vid/avc1/512x270/AtUAgFyBYkGD5VQj.mp4?tag=27
clean_summary: Agent observability aims to improve agent performance, but traditional tools often fail to link traces to meaningful actions. Teams have to manually analyze traces, guess root causes, and write evals. Engine is built to close this loop by monitoring traces, generating ready-to-merge fixes, and writing evals. Now, each trace can lead to a fix, an eval, and a better agent.

everything we build at LangChain is provider/model agnostic for these reasons!

On topic: there is a mistake I saw large companies make in late 2025/early 2026 which is they picked their coding model provider, chat tool, and harness and put the whole company on it. There was a big leap in model ability and folks felt confident.
I have been walking into these teams and they have no idea how good codex is or that notion AI is sick af, of what’s what in the agent world.
And now they’re sunk in a contract AND internal intertia while missing out on the best & most efficient tools of the moment.

clean_summary:
Everything built at LangChain is designed to be provider and model agnostic. Their harness is open source and easily customizable, allowing organizations to remain flexible.

This led to organizations being stuck in contracts and internal inertia, missing out on the best and most efficient tools available.

The key message is to avoid premature convergence on specific tools, as consumer and enterprise options are a gift when competition drives capabilities to improve every month. Keeping options open enables organizations to leverage the rapid progress in AI tools.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: SmithDB: a database optimized for agent observability workloads
summary:
This quote from our friends at @cogent_security says a lot:
“At Cogent, our background agents can produce a huge volume of traces all at once. We need live observability into those systems, and SmithDB has been able to deliver that experience: seeing traces in seconds instead of minutes, which is what we experienced when testing other providers.”
When building SmithDB, we focused heavily not only on query performance but also ingestion performance.
We spent a lot of time meticulously optimizing our ingestion path (batching, compressing, indexing, uploading, etc) to achieve sub-second median write latency.
This is a time it takes for data to be durably stored and become available to queries from the time the data is received.
Waiting tens of second or even minutes for your traces to show up is completely unacceptable.
Quoting @ankush_gola11
We built SmithDB: the database purpose built for agent observability workloads that now powers many parts of LangSmith.
Agent observability presents a challenging data problem. Agent traces can contain tens of thousands of intermediate spans and large, unbounded payloads. These characteristics are a direct result of agents running for longer time horizons and LLM context window sizes growing.
Traditional data infrastructure was not built to handle the complexities associated with storing and querying this data.
SmithDB brings LangSmith up to 12x performance improvements across access patterns most important for agent observability. I’ve been working on SmithDB directly with an amazing team over the past few months, and I’m incredibly proud of the results we’re seeing.
I wrote a bit more about the story and engineering challenges behind SmithDB in this blog.
Additionally, if you’re a systems engineer interested in building the future of agent observability, please reach out!

@ankush_gola11 explains that SmithDB is purpose-built for agent observability, handling complex data like tens of thousands of spans and large payloads, which traditional infrastructure struggles with. The result is up to 12 times performance improvement across key access patterns, supporting the growing needs of long-running agents and expanding LLM context windows. The engineering story and challenges behind SmithDB are detailed in a blog, and system engineers interested in agent observability are encouraged to reach out.

This release is absolutely stacked. I want to call out a sleeper feature: Interpreters
Imagine your cloud agent gets a 10k-row CSV of support tickets. Without a code runtime, the model is stuck reasoning over chunks of raw rows in context

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Two types of evaluation suites for general agents: benchmark and comprehensive coverage
summary:
I've been thinking a lot about the two different groups of evals you need in general agents/agents which handle broad tasks:
1. Benchmark evals - this is a suite of up to 100 eval cases which test the happy paths of your agent, and its most common use cases. This isn't that comprehensive, but covers enough to where you can use it to quickly judge how well your agent handles tasks
2. Test coverage evals - this is a much more detailed suite (maybe up to 500, or more individual cases) that covers every single task you want your agent to be able to handle. It doesn't just include single tests for tasks, but multiple tests per use case, all with slightly different user prompting/tragectories
There needs to be two suites for a few reasons:
- general agents have so many use cases, to accurately test them, and have confidence it preforms well on everything you want to support, you need many evals for each workflow
- the comprehensive eval suite will become too expensive to run on any sort of recurring basis (let alone ci) think $1000's per run, esp if you're supporting multiple models. so you need a smaller suite (the benchmark eval) to quickly gauge whether or not your agent works on code changes
- in general agents, agents can preform the same tasks, but via very different paths. the final result is all the user cares about, but the intermediate steps can look very different. if your eval suite doesn't cover multiple paths to reach the same result, you can't be confident your agent will actually work well in all real world scenarios your users put your agent into
there's a lot more nuance here, so maybe i'll write a longer blog post on it, and how we're thinking about maintaining/building eval suites this large...
clean_summary:
Evaluating general agents that handle broad tasks requires two evaluation suites. The first is a benchmark eval, with up to 100 cases testing the agent's most common use cases and happy paths, allowing quick assessment of performance. The second is a test coverage eval, with over 500 cases covering every task and multiple variations per use case, ensuring the agent can handle all desired workflows.

Having both suites addresses several needs: the comprehensive suite is expensive to run regularly, so the smaller benchmark suite provides a quick check after code changes. Additionally, since agents can perform the same task through different paths, the evaluation suite must cover multiple routes to ensure reliable performance across real-world scenarios.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Using evaluations to measure and improve AI agents before and after deployment
summary:
brain dump of how/why we use Evals to measure agents before & after shipping to prod
1. Good Evals simulate what our real users will do and encounter. They’re not really random benchmark tasks, they reflect our priors on likely user behaviors to make sure the agent passes those cases in the product before we just ship it
2. With that said, the best Evals often aren’t made from scratch, they’re discovered from real world Traces. I’ll literally never ship a perfect agent first try, we need user feedback and failures from Traces to make Evals and then make sure these errors don’t happen again
3. At a basic level, Evals give us some measurable, apples to apples way of comparing performance. Ex: is my agent good today and also in 1 month when I go to try a new model?
4. Evals ~= Environments, we need some place to run Eval Tasks, which is defined by the environment setup. This should mirror prod as much as possible. The more that Eval drifts from prod, the higher my Sim2Real gap and the less I can trust the numbers
5. Evals are our regression tests. Sometimes a prompt change might fix something today while breaking something I changed last week. Evals help us catch that
6. Evals are our training data. They map out what we hope the agent should be & do. We literally fit the agent to evals in hopes of making more Evals pass. Good evals —> good agent. In some rough way:
Agent = fit(model, evals)
7. It’s ok if some Evals fail today if it means this Eval is simply too hard for today’s models, but it’s something to strive towards for the next gen of agents. But you should still do agent engineering today to make them pass if you can, it’s a goal to engineer towards
8. The best Eval is an Eval that actually exists. I think still today Evals are daunting because of the blank canvas problem. “Where do I even start??” But I find small Unit Test style evals are a great place to start to feel like I’m building momentum. I can get a real number + Unit Tests are familiar to many folks
9. Evals need to undergo spring clean. Not every is relevant over time. Models get smarter, agent priorities shift, user behavior shifts. Just how we clean up dead code, we clean up dead evals. This saves us money and avoids us training in agent behaviors we don’t care about anymore
we make Evals not because it’s what everyone says to do, but because it’s one of the most meaningful levers we can pull in building better agents. and if we can help make that easier or at the very least make it less scary to start then that’s great :)
clean_summary: Evaluations (Evals) are essential tools for measuring AI agent performance both before shipping and in production. Good Evals simulate real user behaviors based on priors, ensuring the agent handles likely scenarios. They are often discovered from real-world traces, incorporating user feedback and failures to identify and fix errors. Evals provide a measurable way to compare performance over time and across models, acting as regression tests to catch regressions from prompt changes. They also serve as training data, guiding the agent towards desired behaviors. While some Evals may be too difficult initially, they set goals for future improvements. Starting with small, unit-test-like Evals helps build momentum, and regular cleaning of outdated or irrelevant Evals ensures focus on meaningful metrics. Overall, Evals are a powerful lever for building better agents, making their creation and maintenance less daunting.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Condensing long horizon evaluations with agents into smaller, targeted subsets
summary:
you can condense long horizon evals with agents into smaller subsets that still let you test intended behavior.
i'm currently evaluating an agent that runs for 30+ minutes, and analyzes thousands of traces at a time.
here's my process: if you're evaluating whether X impacts Y agent output, oftentimes a lot of the information that exists in X isn't relevant to the decision of Y.
i extract the reasoning out of trace, and then figure out what is the cause of a specific behavior. then, i know what situation i need to re-create when setting up my eval.
and as a result, i can create a much smaller/simpler version of the long horizon eval that i can quickly use to figure out what i need to change in my prompts to get the behavior i want.
clean_summary: Harrison Chase explains a process for simplifying long horizon evaluations of agents. Instead of analyzing thousands of traces from a 30+ minute run, he extracts reasoning from traces to identify the causes of specific behaviors. This allows recreating relevant situations with smaller, easier-to-analyze setups, enabling quicker testing of how changes in prompts affect the agent's output.

We built SmithDB: the database purpose built for agent observability workloads that now powers many parts of LangSmith.
Agent observability presents a challenging data problem. Agent traces can contain tens of thousands of intermediate spans and large, unbounded payloads. These characteristics are a direct result of agents running for longer time horizons and LLM context window sizes growing.

SmithDB brings LangSmith up to 12x performance improvements across access patterns most important for agent observability. I’ve been working on SmithDB directly with an amazing team over the past few months, and I’m incredibly proud of the results we’re seeing.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Self-optimizing loops in software and agents
summary:
everyone is talking about self-optimizing loops in software & agents. but what does that actually mean?
in my mind, it's a system that observes it's own outputs, evaluates them, and uses that signal to improve itself in the future. the reason why it has become so popular now, is because the evaluation step is finally reliable with llms. this wasn't really the case a year ago.
this is why i'm so bullish on langsmith engine. we've incorporated a ton of different concepts that allow developers to invest in this self-optimizing loop that makes the improvement flywheel spin faster & faster.
some examples of this include
> feedback you leave on traces are automatically triaged
> every fix that we suggest has an online evaluator, so you never regress
> we create offline evals that you can add to your test suite
> we continually learn on your preferences, and tune our evaluation & fix step based on this
and we're seeing crazy adoption, and lots of growth across our customers. it is truly something that just gets better the more time you spend on it.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJQhP60WAAAuc5e.png
clean_summary:
Everyone is talking about self-optimizing loops in software and agents, which are systems that observe their own outputs, evaluate them, and use that feedback to improve themselves over time. Their popularity has grown because large language models now make the evaluation step reliable, which wasn't the case a year ago.

The LangSmith engine exemplifies this approach by integrating concepts that accelerate the self-improvement cycle. Features include automatic triaging of feedback traces, online evaluators for suggested fixes to prevent regressions, offline evaluations for test suites, and continual learning from user preferences to refine evaluation and fixing processes. Adoption is rapidly increasing, and the system improves with more use.

langsmith engine is an agent that helps you spin the optimization loop for your own agents

everyone is talking about self-optimizing loops in software & agents. but what does that actually mean?
in my mind, it's a system that observes it's own outputs, evaluates them, and uses that signal to improve itself in the future. the reason why it has become so popular now, is because the evaluation step is finally reliable with llms. this wasn't really the case a year ago.
this is why i'm so bullish on langsmith engine. we've incorporated a ton of different concepts that allow developers to invest in this self-optimizing loop that makes the improvement flywheel spin faster & faster.
some examples of this include
> feedback you leave on traces are automatically triaged
> every fix that we suggest has an online evaluator, so you never regress
> we create offline evals that you can add to your test suite
> we continually learn on your preferences, and tune our evaluation & fix step based on this

Langsmith engine is an agent that helps you spin the optimization loop for your own agents. It facilitates systems that observe their outputs, evaluate them, and use that feedback to improve over time. The recent reliability of LLM-based evaluation makes this approach more practical now than it was a year ago.

The engine incorporates concepts like automatic triaging of feedback, online evaluators for suggested fixes, offline evals for test suites, and continual learning from user preferences. These features accelerate the self-improvement cycle, leading to widespread adoption and growth among users, as the system gets better the more it is used.

experiments
loop

clean_title: Self-optimizing loops with LangSmith Engine improve multi-agent workflows
summary:
Completely agree, @hwchase17 !
This is the meta-level breakthrough we've all been waiting for.
Self-optimizing loops finally feel production-ready because LangSmith Engine turns evaluation from a manual chore into a reliable, always-on flywheel.
I've been running it on a multi-agent research workflow (POC) for the past couple weeks, and the difference is night and day.
Many unknowns, what used to take me days of manual debugging and A/B testing now iterates in hours: trace feedback gets auto-triaged, suggested fixes come with online evaluators that actually prevent regressions, and the offline evals slot straight into my test suite.
Most impressively, it learns my preferences over time and keeps sharpening the eval/fix steps.
Huge kudos to the LangChain team.
I am sharing a few key points, based on my experience and architectural understanding, for everyone's benefits or any corrections.
Feedback Triage: User thumbs-up/down or comments on traces are automatically routed and prioritized. In my experience, this surfaces the highest-impact issues first instead of drowning in noise.
Online Evaluators on Fixes: Every proposed change ships with a guardrail evaluator. Personally, this saved me from at least 3 regressions in one workflow, super valuable for confidence in production. Auto-generated Pull Requests are just WOW !
Offline Eval Generation: It creates reusable test cases you can add to CI. I integrated these into my LangGraph pipelines and saw test coverage jump without extra manual effort.
Preference Learning: Continuously tunes its own evaluation and suggestion models based on your historical feedback.
Over 2 weeks, I noticed it started aligning better with my style (e.g., favoring certain prompting patterns or tool-use guardrails).
Integration with LangGraph: Works natively with checkpointing and state management, so reward signals and optimization history persist across runs/sessions. Feels like giving your graph a "manager" agent that watches and tunes it.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Model-Harness-Task fit in reinforcement learning and prompting
summary:
Model-Harness-Task fit!
it’s clear that RL post-training produces a model-harness fit via tool shapes and prompting as models are trained with the harness in the loop. Mentioned this in a previous LangChain blog, Cursor also has good content on this
But there’s probably less talk on the importance + experimentation of Harness-Task fit. Practically this includes choices like domain specific prompting (ex: verification coding tasks) or omission of confusing context that doesn’t apply to the current task
Claude Code’s harness has TONS of instructions because they’re forced to serve a very general persona of user who could ask for…anything basically. But there’s a large benefit of using a laser focused set of context and tools relevant to the narrow task at hand without all the other junk
This is the Harness-Task fit
Every component of a harness exists to elicit some behavior from the model. If these components are tuned to the task, then the model benefits. If they’re a mix of noise and good content, the model may be fine but it may get confused
This is why the best vertical AI teams in the world build very bespoke harnesses and evals for their agents
Task-Harness fit helps you rock at the exact thing your customers care about and is why builders can outperform natively post-trained harnesses
Quoting @saurabh_shah2
Question for harness heads: how is it possible that another harness helps a model more than the one it was RL’d against on a top-priority capability?
Not a dunk, I just find this really really surprising !!
clean_summary:
RL post-training produces a model-harness fit through tool shapes and prompting, especially when the harness is tuned to the specific task. Practical choices like domain-specific prompting or omitting irrelevant context can improve performance by aligning the harness with the task at hand.

Every component of a harness aims to elicit certain behaviors from the model; tuning these components to the task benefits the model, while noise can cause confusion. Top AI teams often build bespoke harnesses and evaluations to optimize for their specific applications.

Task-Harness fit enables models to excel at what users care about, which explains why builders can outperform models with natively post-trained harnesses.

@Saurabh_shah2 questions how a different harness can improve a model more than the one used during RL, which is surprising given the importance of task-specific tuning.

title: Harrison Chase (@hwchase17)
clean_title: Building flexible agent harnesses with a worker model instead of frameworks
summary:
Almost everyone is building agent harness systems the wrong way.
The default move: pick LangChain or LangGraph or the OpenAI Agents SDK, accept the loop, the tools, the memory, the orchestration, the policy engine, the credential store, the budget tracker, all of it, as one decision.
Mike, wrote a long piece today on why this shape is wrong, and why every long-running agent team eventually ends up rewriting its harness from scratch.
His argument: a harness isn't one thing. It's fifteen separate concerns bundled together because the surrounding ecosystem didn't give you a way to compose them. Turn state machines, provider routing, credential vaults, policy engines, approval gates, budget trackers, hook fanout, context compaction, session trees, OpenTelemetry tracing. Frameworks ship them as one block because that was the only shape available a year ago.
It isn't anymore.
When every layer is a worker on a shared bus with a typed function contract, "build your own harness" stops meaning "fork a framework." It means swap a worker. Don't like the model catalogue? Write one that hits a live API. Don't like file-backed credentials? Plug in your secrets manager. Want approvals routed through Slack instead of a console? Add a worker that calls approval::resolve. The rest of the stack does not change.
The framework era picked a position for you and locked you in. The worker model leaves the choice in your hand.
Worth reading in full.
Quoting @mfpiccolo
clean_summary: Almost everyone is building agent harness systems the wrong way. The common approach is to accept a monolithic framework like LangChain or OpenAI Agents SDK, which bundles all concerns—loop, tools, memory, orchestration, policy engine, credential store, and more—into one decision. Mike argues that a harness isn't one thing but fifteen separate concerns that should be composable. Instead of a fixed framework, using a worker model where each layer is a worker on a shared bus allows for easy swapping and customization, such as replacing the model catalog, secrets manager, or approval routing without changing the rest of the stack. This shift from framework lock-in to a worker-based approach empowers developers to tailor their agent systems more flexibly.
